bio_edx.7.0.summary: All organisms must move substances such as **oxygen, carbon dioxide, water, dissolved food molecules, mineral ions and urea** into and out of their cells. A single-celled organism has a **large surface area to volume ratio** and short diffusion distances, so diffusion across its surface is enough. As organisms get bigger their **surface area to volume ratio falls** and diffusion distances become too long, so multicellular organisms need specialised **exchange surfaces** (alveoli, villi, root hairs, leaves) and **transport systems** (blood circulation, xylem and phloem) to supply every cell fast enough.

core.p: Every living cell needs a supply of raw materials and must get rid of waste. These substances move between the cells and the environment, and between different parts of an organism.
bullets: **Oxygen** in, for aerobic respiration
**Carbon dioxide** out, a waste product of respiration (and taken in by plants for photosynthesis)
**Water** in, for reactions and to keep cells turgid; excess water out
**Dissolved food molecules** (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids) in, for respiration and growth
**Mineral ions** in, e.g. nitrate for proteins in plants, iron for haemoglobin
**Urea** out, the nitrogenous waste made in the liver

callouts.p: Learn the spec list: oxygen, carbon dioxide, water, dissolved food molecules, mineral ions and urea.

core.p: Substances cross cell membranes by **diffusion**, **osmosis** and **active transport**. Diffusion and osmosis are passive and only work well over **short distances**.
bullets: **Diffusion**: net movement of particles from high to low concentration, down a concentration gradient
**Osmosis**: net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane from a dilute to a more concentrated solution
**Active transport**: movement against a concentration gradient, needing energy from respiration
Diffusion time increases sharply with distance, so it is only fast over a few cells

callouts.p: The net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.

core.p: The **surface area (SA)** of an organism controls how fast substances can be exchanged. The **volume (V)** controls how much it needs. The **SA:V ratio** compares the two.
bullets: SA = total area of all faces (for a cube: 6 x side x side)
V = space inside (for a cube: side x side x side)
SA:V ratio = SA divided by V, written as **x : 1**
A **larger ratio** means more surface for each unit of volume
Small objects have a **large** SA:V ratio; large objects have a **small** one

callouts.p: The surface area of an organism divided by its volume; it decreases as size increases.

core.p: You must be able to calculate SA:V ratio. Work out surface area, then volume, then divide.
bullets: 1 cm cube: SA = 6 x 1 x 1 = 6 cm2; V = 1 cm3; ratio **6 : 1**
2 cm cube: SA = 6 x 2 x 2 = 24 cm2; V = 8 cm3; ratio 24/8 = **3 : 1**
3 cm cube: SA = 6 x 3 x 3 = 54 cm2; V = 27 cm3; ratio **2 : 1**
4 cm cube: SA = 96 cm2; V = 64 cm3; ratio **1.5 : 1**
For a cube, SA:V = 6 / side length, so doubling the side halves the ratio

callouts.p: Surface area is in cm2 and volume in cm3. The ratio itself has no units.

core.p: For a cuboid of length l, width w and height h, there are three pairs of identical faces.
bullets: SA = 2(lw + lh + wh)
V = l x w x h
A flat, thin shape has a larger SA:V than a cube of the same volume

callouts.p: A cube has 6 faces. Students often forget faces they cannot see in the drawing.

core.h: Why SA:V falls as size increases
core.p: Surface area depends on **length squared**, but volume depends on **length cubed**. When an organism gets bigger, its volume grows faster than its surface, so each cm2 of surface has to serve more cm3 of cells.
bullets: Double the length: SA x 4, volume x 8
So the ratio halves
Bigger organisms need more oxygen and food in total (more volume) but have relatively less surface to absorb it
The centre of a large organism is also **far from the surface**

callouts.p: Volume increases faster than surface area as size increases, so SA:V decreases.

core.p: An organism like **Amoeba** or a bacterium is tiny, so it has a **very large SA:V ratio** and every part of the cell is very close to the surface.
bullets: Oxygen and food diffuse in directly across the **cell membrane**
Carbon dioxide and waste diffuse straight out
**Short diffusion distance**, so diffusion is fast enough to meet the cell's needs
No specialised exchange organs or transport system are needed

core.p: In a large organism, most cells are **deep inside**, many cells away from the surface. Its **small SA:V ratio** means the body surface is too small to absorb enough oxygen and food for all its volume.
bullets: **Small SA:V** ratio: not enough surface to supply the whole volume
**Long diffusion distance** to inner cells: diffusion would take far too long
Many organisms have a waterproof or protective outer layer (skin, waxy cuticle) that limits exchange
Larger, active animals have **high metabolic rates**, so need oxygen and glucose quickly
Without help, inner cells would run out of oxygen and build up toxic waste

callouts.p: Small SA:V ratio and long diffusion distances mean diffusion across the body surface alone is too slow for multicellular organisms.

core.p: Multicellular organisms have organs with a **very large surface area** packed into a small space, so they can exchange materials fast enough.
bullets: **Alveoli** in the lungs: oxygen in, carbon dioxide out
**Villi** in the small intestine: absorb digested food molecules
**Root hair cells** in plants: absorb water and mineral ions
**Leaves**: flat and thin with stomata for gas exchange
**Gills** in fish: gas exchange with water
Common features: **large surface area, thin (short diffusion distance), good supply/transport to keep a steep concentration gradient**

head: Exchange surface
Organism
Substances exchanged
rows: Glucose, amino acids, fatty acids in
CO2 in, O2 and water vapour out

core.p: An exchange surface is only useful if the substances absorbed can be carried quickly to every cell. A **transport system** moves substances by **mass flow** over long distances, so each cell is only a short diffusion distance from a supply.
bullets: Humans: **circulatory system** – heart pumps blood through arteries, capillaries and veins
Blood carries oxygen (red blood cells) and dissolved food, CO2, urea and hormones (plasma)
**Capillaries** reach close to every cell, so diffusion distances are short
Plants: **xylem** carries water and mineral ions from roots to leaves
Plants: **phloem** carries dissolved sugars (sucrose) around the plant
Transport also keeps **concentration gradients steep** at exchange surfaces by carrying substances away

callouts.p: Exam answers score highest when they link the exchange surface (gets substances in) to the transport system (gets them to every cell).

core.p: Bigger and more active organisms need more complex systems. Insects, mammals and birds all have different solutions, but the reason is always SA:V and distance.
bullets: Flatworms are very flat, giving a **large SA:V** and short distances, so they need no lungs or blood system
Mammals and birds keep a constant body temperature, so need more respiration and more oxygen
Small mammals lose heat quickly because of their large SA:V ratio
Elephants have a small SA:V and use large ears to increase surface area for heat loss

callouts.p: A flat shape can have a high SA:V even if the organism is large, which is why leaves are thin and flat.

core.p: Edexcel questions ask you to calculate SA:V, interpret data, and explain why organisms need exchange surfaces and transport systems.
bullets: Calculate SA and volume for cubes and cuboids
Express ratios as x : 1 (divide both by the volume)
Compare ratios and conclude which organism exchanges faster per unit volume
Explain using **surface area, volume, diffusion distance and rate of diffusion**
A practical model: agar cubes with indicator in acid – smaller cubes change colour completely faster

callouts.p: Cut cubes of agar containing indicator, place in acid and time how long until the colour changes all the way through. Smaller cubes (larger SA:V) change faster.

analogy.t: Feeding a crowd through the doors of a building
analogy.p: Imagine food is delivered through the doors on the outside of a building (surface area), and the people inside (volume) all need feeding. A tiny hut has lots of doors for a few people, and everyone is near a door. A huge stadium has far more people for each door, and people in the middle are a long walk away. So the stadium builds extra serving hatches with many windows (exchange surfaces like alveoli and villi) and a conveyor belt running to every seat (the circulatory system). Where it breaks down: people walk with purpose, but diffusion is random movement of particles, and real organisms also need waste carried out, not just food in.

terms.d: A specialised surface where substances move into or out of an organism, such as alveoli, villi or root hairs.
A system that moves substances by mass flow to all parts of an organism, e.g. blood circulation, xylem and phloem.
The total area of the outside of an object, measured in cm2.
The amount of space an object takes up, measured in cm3.
Surface area divided by volume; it decreases as an organism gets larger.
Net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration.
The difference in concentration between two areas; a steeper gradient gives faster diffusion.
How far a substance must travel; shorter distances give faster diffusion.
Net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane from a dilute to a more concentrated solution.
Movement of substances against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration.
Made of many cells, with most cells far from the body surface.
Made of one cell, with a large SA:V ratio and short diffusion distances.
Tiny air sacs in the lungs that give a huge surface area for gas exchange.
Finger-like projections in the small intestine that increase surface area for absorbing food molecules.
Plant tissue that transports water and mineral ions from the roots.
Plant tissue that transports dissolved sugars around the plant.
Nitrogenous waste made in the liver that must be transported to the kidneys for excretion.

mistakes.w: Larger organisms have a larger surface area to volume ratio.
mistakes.r: Larger organisms have a **smaller** SA:V ratio, even though their actual surface area is bigger.

mistakes.w: Big organisms need transport systems because they have a small surface area.
mistakes.r: They have a small surface area **relative to volume** (small SA:V) and **long diffusion distances**.

mistakes.w: Writing the ratio as 24:8.
mistakes.r: Simplify to **3 : 1** by dividing by the volume.

mistakes.w: Surface area of a cube = side x side.
mistakes.r: SA of a cube = **6 x side x side** (six faces).

mistakes.w: Diffusion is too slow because there is not enough oxygen.
mistakes.r: Diffusion is too slow because the **distance** to inner cells is too great and SA:V is too small.

mistakes.w: Exchange surfaces are thick to protect them.
mistakes.r: Exchange surfaces are **thin** to give a short diffusion distance.

mistakes.w: Single-celled organisms need a transport system.
mistakes.r: They have a **large SA:V** ratio and short distances, so diffusion across the membrane is enough.

mistakes.w: As size doubles, SA:V halves because surface area halves.
mistakes.r: SA increases x4 and volume x8, so volume increases **faster**, which halves the ratio.

exam.q: State what happens to the surface area to volume ratio as an organism gets larger.
model: It decreases
exam.tip: One word is enough, but say decreases not changes.

exam.q: Name two substances that must be transported into cells and one that must be removed.
model: Any two of: oxygen, glucose / dissolved food, water, mineral ions
Removed: carbon dioxide or urea
exam.tip: Use the spec list.

exam.q: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube with sides of 5 cm.
model: SA = 6 x 5 x 5 = 150 cm2 and V = 125 cm3
exam.tip: Show both SA and volume.

exam.q: A cuboid cell model measures 1 cm x 2 cm x 4 cm. Calculate its SA:V ratio.
model: V = 8 cm3
exam.tip: List the three different face areas and double the total.

exam.q: Explain why a single-celled organism does not need a transport system.
model: Large surface area to volume ratio
Short diffusion distance so diffusion across membrane is fast enough to meet needs
exam.tip: Mention both ratio and distance.

exam.q: Explain why multicellular organisms need exchange surfaces.
model: Small surface area to volume ratio / body surface too small for volume
Exchange surfaces give a large surface area to absorb substances fast enough
exam.tip: Name an example such as alveoli or villi for clarity.

exam.q: Explain why a mammal needs a circulatory system.
model: Mammal is large / multicellular with small SA:V ratio
Long diffusion distance from surface to inner cells
Diffusion alone would be too slow to supply oxygen and glucose / remove CO2
Blood transports substances to all cells by mass flow / capillaries close to cells
exam.tip: Explain the problem, then the solution.

exam.q: Students placed agar cubes of side 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm containing indicator in acid. Predict and explain which cube changed colour completely first.
model: The 1 cm cube
It has the largest SA:V ratio
Acid has the shortest distance to diffuse to the centre
exam.tip: Link prediction to SA:V and distance.

exam.q: Describe how the SA:V ratio changes when the side of a cube is doubled, and explain why.
model: The ratio halves
Surface area increases x4 but volume increases x8 / volume increases faster than SA
exam.tip: Use numbers to prove it.

exam.q: Explain why large multicellular organisms need both specialised exchange surfaces and a transport system. Use examples from animals and plants.
model: Cells need oxygen, glucose, water, mineral ions; must remove CO2 and urea
Large organisms have a small SA:V ratio, so body surface cannot exchange enough
Long diffusion distances to inner cells make diffusion too slow
Exchange surfaces such as alveoli, villi and root hairs provide large surface area and thin walls
Transport system (blood, heart, capillaries) carries substances to every cell
In plants xylem carries water and ions, phloem carries sugars
Transport keeps concentration gradients steep at exchange surfaces
exam.tip: Cover need, problem, exchange surfaces, transport and at least one plant and one animal example.

worked.q: Calculate and compare the SA:V ratios of a 2 cm cube and a 6 cm cube.
steps: 2 cm cube: SA = 6 x 2 x 2 = 24 cm2
6 cm cube: SA = 6 x 6 x 6 = 216 cm2
Compare: 3 / 1 = 3 times larger for the small cube
worked.ans: 2 cm cube = 3 : 1; 6 cm cube = 1 : 1. The smaller cube has three times as much surface per unit volume.

worked.q: A flatworm is 10 mm long, 5 mm wide and 0.5 mm thick. Calculate its SA:V ratio and explain why it does not need a circulatory system.
steps: Flat body: no cell is more than 0.25 mm from the surface
worked.ans: SA:V = 4.6 : 1. Its large SA:V and very short diffusion distance mean diffusion across the body surface supplies all cells.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why an Amoeba can rely on diffusion but a human cannot.
steps: Amoeba is a single cell, very small, with a large SA:V ratio
Every part is close to the membrane, so the diffusion distance is short
A human has trillions of cells and a small SA:V ratio
Inner cells are many cells away from the surface, so diffusion would be far too slow
Humans therefore have lungs (alveoli) and small intestine (villi) and a circulatory system
worked.ans: Amoeba has a large SA:V and short distances; a human has a small SA:V and long distances, so needs exchange surfaces and a transport system.

bio_edx.7.1.summary: Gas exchange in the lungs happens in millions of tiny air sacs called **alveoli**, where **oxygen diffuses** from the air into the blood and **carbon dioxide diffuses** from the blood into the air. Alveoli are adapted to make diffusion as fast as possible: they give a **huge surface area**, have **walls one cell thick** with thin capillary walls next to them (a **short diffusion distance**), a **moist lining**, and a **rich capillary network** plus **ventilation** that keep a **steep concentration gradient**. Every adaptation links to increasing the rate of diffusion.

core.p: Air enters through the nose and mouth, passes down the **trachea**, into two **bronchi**, then branches into smaller and smaller **bronchioles**, which end in clusters of **alveoli**. Gas exchange happens only in the alveoli.
bullets: Trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → **alveoli**
The trachea is held open by rings of **cartilage**
Each lung contains hundreds of millions of alveoli
The alveoli are surrounded by a dense network of **capillaries**
The lungs are inside the thorax, protected by the ribs, above the diaphragm

callouts.p: A tiny air sac in the lungs where gas exchange takes place by diffusion (plural: alveoli).

fig.cap: The airways branch like an upside-down tree: the trachea splits into two bronchi, which divide into many bronchioles ending in clusters of alveoli, where gas exchange occurs.

core.p: Air in the alveolus has a **high concentration of oxygen** and a **low concentration of carbon dioxide**. Blood arriving in the capillaries from the body (via the pulmonary artery) has **low oxygen** and **high carbon dioxide**. Each gas diffuses down its own concentration gradient.
bullets: **Oxygen** diffuses from the air in the alveolus into the blood in the capillary
It then enters **red blood cells** and binds to **haemoglobin**
**Carbon dioxide** diffuses from the blood plasma into the alveolus
Carbon dioxide is then breathed out
Blood leaving the lungs (pulmonary vein) is **oxygenated**

callouts.p: Oxygen moves in and carbon dioxide moves out at the same time, each down its own concentration gradient.

core.p: Hundreds of millions of tiny alveoli give the lungs a total surface area of roughly a tennis court, packed into the chest. More surface means more gas can diffuse at the same time.
bullets: Many small, spherical alveoli give a **very large surface area**
Their shape increases surface area to volume ratio compared with one big sac
More area → **more molecules cross per second** → faster rate of diffusion
Lets enough oxygen enter for the high respiration rate of a large, warm-blooded mammal

callouts.p: Never just list 'large surface area' – add 'so more oxygen can diffuse into the blood at once / faster rate of diffusion'.

core.h: Adaptation 2: thin walls and short diffusion distance
core.p: The wall of each alveolus is made of a single layer of **flattened cells**, and so is the capillary wall pressed right against it. Together they make a very **short diffusion distance** between air and blood.
bullets: Alveolus wall is **one cell thick** (thin, flattened cells)
Capillary wall is also **one cell thick**
Capillaries are in **close contact** with the alveolus wall
Oxygen only crosses about two thin cells to reach the blood
Shorter distance → **faster diffusion**

callouts.p: Animal cells have no cell walls. The 'wall' of an alveolus is a layer of cells; say 'one cell thick', not 'thin cell wall'.

core.p: The inner surface of each alveolus is covered with a **thin layer of moisture**. Oxygen **dissolves** in this water before it diffuses across the cell membranes.
bullets: Gases must **dissolve** to diffuse across cell membranes
The moist lining allows oxygen to dissolve quickly
Moisture is kept thin so it does not add much to the diffusion distance
A consequence: we lose water vapour when we breathe out

core.p: Each alveolus is wrapped in a **dense network of capillaries**. Blood flows through constantly, carrying oxygen away and bringing carbon dioxide, so the concentration gradient stays steep.
bullets: Blood **constantly removes oxygen** from the alveolar area
So oxygen concentration in the capillary stays **lower** than in the air
Blood **constantly brings carbon dioxide**, keeping its concentration higher in the blood
**Haemoglobin** binds oxygen, so dissolved oxygen in plasma stays low, keeping the gradient steep
Capillaries are narrow, so red blood cells pass slowly and close to the wall

callouts.p: A good blood supply maintains a steep concentration gradient, which keeps diffusion fast.

core.p: Breathing in and out (**ventilation**) constantly replaces the air in the alveoli. Fresh air brings in more oxygen and stale air takes away carbon dioxide.
bullets: Breathing in: fresh air with **high oxygen** concentration enters the alveoli
Breathing out: air with **high carbon dioxide** concentration leaves
Keeps oxygen concentration in alveoli **higher** than in blood
Keeps carbon dioxide concentration in alveoli **lower** than in blood
Ventilation + blood flow together maintain the gradients from both sides

core.p: Every adaptation of the alveoli increases the **rate of diffusion**. Learn each feature with how it helps.
bullets: Use the format: **feature → effect on diffusion**
Large surface area → more gas exchanged at once
Thin walls → short diffusion distance
Rich blood supply and ventilation → steep concentration gradient

callouts.p: In a 4-mark 'explain how alveoli are adapted' question, give two features each with its reason.

core.p: Comparing the air we breathe in and out shows that gas exchange has happened.
bullets: Oxygen falls from about 21% to about 16%
Carbon dioxide rises from about 0.04% to about 4%
Nitrogen stays about 78%, as it is not used
Exhaled air is warmer and contains more water vapour

callouts.p: Not all oxygen is absorbed; exhaled air still contains about 16% oxygen.

core.p: Gas exchange in the alveoli is entirely **passive**. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are small molecules that diffuse through cell membranes down their concentration gradients, so no energy from respiration is needed.
bullets: Diffusion is **passive**: no ATP used
Oxygen and carbon dioxide are small, so pass straight through membranes
The direction depends only on the **concentration gradient**
If the gradient were reversed, gases would diffuse the other way

callouts.p: Never say oxygen is actively transported into the blood in the lungs.

core.p: Diseases that reduce surface area or increase diffusion distance cut the rate of gas exchange, which shows why the adaptations matter.
bullets: **Emphysema** (often from smoking): alveolus walls break down, forming fewer, larger air spaces → **smaller surface area**
Less oxygen diffuses into blood, so people are breathless and tired
Fluid or thickened tissue in the lungs **increases diffusion distance**
Smoking tar coats surfaces and damages cilia in the airways

callouts.p: For any unfamiliar disease, ask: does it change surface area, distance or gradient? Then explain the effect on diffusion.

analogy.t: A busy station with thousands of ticket gates
analogy.p: The alveoli are like a station with thousands of ticket gates (huge surface area). Each gate is just a thin turnstile to walk through (short diffusion distance). Trains on the platform (capillaries) keep carrying passengers away so the platform never gets crowded, while new crowds keep arriving at the entrance (ventilation), so people always flow in one direction (steep gradient). Where it breaks down: passengers choose where to go, but gas molecules move randomly; the net flow happens only because there are more molecules on one side. Also, in the lungs carbon dioxide passengers are leaving through the same gates at the same time.

worked.q: Applied example: Explain why fluid building up in the alveoli (as in pneumonia) reduces oxygen levels in the blood.

Some alveoli fill completely, reducing the surface area available
So the rate of diffusion of oxygen into the blood falls

bio_edx.7.2.summary: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration, and it is passive, so it needs no energy from respiration. Its rate depends on three main factors: the surface area available, the size of the concentration gradient, and the diffusion distance (thickness of the membrane). Fick's law links these together: rate of diffusion is proportional to (surface area x concentration difference) / thickness of membrane, which explains why exchange surfaces such as alveoli, villi and gills are large, thin and well supplied with blood.

core.p: Particles in liquids and gases move about randomly all the time. When there are more particles in one place than another, more of them happen to move from the crowded area to the less crowded area than the other way, so there is a **net movement** down the **concentration gradient**.
bullets: Diffusion is **passive**: it uses the kinetic energy of the particles, not energy from respiration (no ATP).
It happens in gases and in liquids (solutions), and across **partially permeable membranes** if the particles are small enough.
Particles still move in both directions; the word **net** means overall more go one way.
Diffusion stops being net (dynamic equilibrium) when concentrations are equal on both sides.
Examples in animals: oxygen from alveoli into blood, carbon dioxide from blood into alveoli, digested food (e.g. glucose) from the small intestine into the blood, urea from cells into the blood.

callouts.p: The net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration, down a concentration gradient. It is a passive process.

core.h: The three factors in the spec
core.p: Edexcel expects you to explain how **surface area**, **concentration gradient** and **diffusion distance** affect the rate of diffusion, and to link each one to the structure of exchange surfaces.
bullets: Larger **surface area**: more particles can cross at the same time, so rate increases.
Steeper (bigger) **concentration gradient**: a bigger difference in concentration means many more particles move one way than the other each second, so rate increases.
Shorter **diffusion distance** (thinner membrane): particles have less distance to travel, so they cross faster and the rate increases.
Temperature also affects the rate: particles have more kinetic energy and move faster when warmer, but in mammals body temperature is kept roughly constant at about 37 °C.

head: Factor
Change that increases rate
Why
rows: More area for particles to cross at once
More net particles move per second

callouts.p: Big surface area, steep gradient, short distance. Every exchange surface question comes back to these.

core.p: The rate of diffusion is directly proportional to surface area. If you double the surface area (with everything else the same) you double the rate, because twice as many particles can cross the membrane at once.
bullets: Lungs have about 300-500 million **alveoli**, giving a total surface area of roughly 70 m² (about half a tennis court).
Small intestine has **villi** and **microvilli** which greatly increase its surface area for absorbing digested food.
Fish gills have many **gill filaments** and **lamellae** for a large surface area.
Folding a surface increases the surface area without making the organ much bigger.
Large organisms have a small **surface area to volume ratio**, so they need specialised exchange surfaces to make up for it.

callouts.p: Only say 'doubles' if the question says all other factors are kept the same.

core.p: The rate of diffusion is directly proportional to the **concentration difference** across the membrane. A bigger difference means a steeper gradient and faster net movement.
bullets: In the lungs, **breathing (ventilation)** keeps bringing in fresh air high in oxygen and removing air high in carbon dioxide.
**Blood flow** in the capillaries constantly carries oxygenated blood away and brings deoxygenated blood, so oxygen concentration in the blood next to the alveolus stays low.
Together, ventilation and blood flow **maintain** a steep concentration gradient, so diffusion never slows to a stop.
In the small intestine, the blood supply in each villus carries absorbed glucose away, keeping the gradient steep.
If the gradient is reversed, net diffusion goes the other way.

callouts.p: Mark schemes reward 'a good blood supply maintains a steep concentration gradient', not just 'a good blood supply'.

core.p: The rate of diffusion is **inversely proportional** to the thickness of the membrane (the diffusion distance). If the distance is halved, the rate doubles.
bullets: Alveolus walls are **one cell thick** and made of flattened (squamous) cells.
Capillary walls are also **one cell thick**, and capillaries press right against the alveolus.
So the total distance for oxygen from air to red blood cell is very small, about 1 µm or less.
Moist lining: gases dissolve in the thin layer of moisture before diffusing across.
Diseases that thicken the membrane (e.g. fibrosis) reduce the rate of gas exchange, so people become breathless.

callouts.p: Thicker membrane means slower diffusion. Thinner membrane means faster diffusion.

core.p: Fick's law puts all three factors into one relationship. You need to be able to write it, use it in calculations, and use it to explain the structure of exchange surfaces.
bullets: rate of diffusion ∝ (surface area x concentration difference) / thickness of membrane
The symbol ∝ means 'is proportional to'.
Surface area and concentration difference are on the **top** (numerator), so increasing them increases rate.
Thickness of membrane is on the **bottom** (denominator), so increasing it decreases rate.
Because it is a proportionality, the answer is often in arbitrary units (au), or used as a ratio to compare two situations.

callouts.p: Rate of diffusion ∝ (surface area x concentration difference) / thickness of membrane.

core.p: To calculate, multiply surface area by concentration difference, then divide by thickness. Keep units consistent. To compare two situations, work out the rate for each, or work out the factor each variable changes by.
bullets: Step 1: write the formula.
Step 2: substitute the numbers, with the same units for both situations.
Step 3: calculate and give units (often arbitrary units) and a sensible number of significant figures.
Factor method: new rate = old rate x (area factor) x (gradient factor) / (thickness factor).
Example: area doubled and thickness doubled gives no change in rate (x2 / 2 = 1).
Example: gradient halved and thickness halved gives no change in rate.

callouts.p: Calculation questions give a mark for the correct substitution even if the final answer is wrong.

core.h: Applying the factors to the alveoli
core.p: Alveoli are the classic exchange surface. Every one of their features links back to a term in Fick's law.
bullets: Huge numbers of alveoli give a **large surface area** (top of Fick's law).
**Thin walls, one cell thick**, plus thin capillary walls give a **short diffusion distance** (bottom of Fick's law).
**Rich capillary network** and continuous blood flow, plus ventilation, **maintain a steep concentration gradient** (top of Fick's law).
Moist surface lets gases dissolve before diffusing.
Result: oxygen diffuses quickly into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses quickly out.

core.p: The same three factors explain the structure of exchange surfaces all over the living world. Use the same Fick's law reasoning in unfamiliar contexts.
bullets: **Villi** in the small intestine: large surface area (villi and microvilli), thin wall one cell thick, good blood supply keeps the gradient steep.
**Fish gills**: many filaments and lamellae (large area), thin lamellae, blood flows in the opposite direction to water (countercurrent) to keep a gradient along the whole gill.
**Leaves**: large flat surface, many stomata, air spaces in the spongy mesophyll, thin leaves give a short distance.
**Placenta**: many villi increase surface area, thin barrier between mother's and fetus's blood.

callouts.p: Find the large surface area, the short distance and what keeps the gradient steep. That is usually 3 marks.

core.h: Why surface area to volume ratio matters
core.p: As an organism gets bigger, its volume increases faster than its surface area, so its **surface area to volume ratio** falls. Diffusion across the body surface alone is too slow to supply all its cells.
bullets: Single-celled organisms have a large SA:V ratio and short diffusion distances, so diffusion across the cell membrane is enough.
Large multicellular organisms need specialised exchange surfaces (lungs, gills, villi) to increase surface area.
They also need a **transport system** (blood and heart) to carry substances over long distances and to maintain gradients.
Fick's law shows why: rate depends on area, so a low area for a large volume gives too low a rate.

core.h: Explaining effects of disease and lifestyle
core.p: Exam questions often ask you to use Fick's law to explain why a person with a condition is breathless or tired.
bullets: **Emphysema** (often from smoking): alveolus walls break down, forming fewer, larger air spaces, so **surface area decreases** and rate of diffusion falls.
**Fibrosis** or fluid build-up: membrane becomes thicker, so **diffusion distance increases** and rate falls.
Less oxygen reaches the blood, so less oxygen gets to cells for aerobic respiration; less energy is released, so the person feels tired.
At high altitude there is less oxygen in the air, so the **concentration gradient is smaller**.
Exercise: faster breathing and faster heart rate increase the concentration gradient, so gas exchange speeds up.

callouts.p: Write 'less energy is released (transferred) by respiration', never 'less energy is produced'.

core.p: Most marks on this point come from linking a feature to a factor and then to the rate. Use the chain: feature, then factor, then effect on rate.
bullets: Chain example: 'Walls are one cell thick, so short diffusion distance, so faster diffusion of oxygen.'
Always name the substance and direction (e.g. oxygen into the blood).
Use the words **net**, **concentration gradient** and **rate**.
For 6-mark questions, cover all three factors and give a specific structure for each.
In calculations, state the formula, substitute, calculate, and give units.

callouts.p: Write 'larger surface area' or 'shorter distance', not just 'large' or 'short', when comparing two organisms or surfaces.

analogy.t: A crowded room emptying into a hall
analogy.p: Imagine a packed classroom with doors into an empty hall. People wander randomly, so more end up in the hall than come back (net movement down a gradient). More doors (surface area) let more people through at once. A more packed room compared to the hall (steeper gradient) means more net flow. A short doorway rather than a long corridor (short distance) means people get through quicker. Where it breaks down: people choose where to go, but particles move completely randomly with no purpose, and particles do not get tired or need energy to keep moving.

terms.d: The net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration, down a concentration gradient; a passive process.
Not requiring energy from respiration.
The difference in concentration of a substance between two areas.
The value used in Fick's law: concentration on one side of the membrane minus concentration on the other.
The total area of a surface across which particles can be exchanged.
The distance particles must travel, for example the thickness of the membrane or cells they cross.
Rate of diffusion ∝ (surface area x concentration difference) / thickness of membrane.
When one quantity doubles, the other doubles.
When one quantity doubles, the other halves.
A membrane that lets some small molecules through but not others.
Tiny air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange happens by diffusion.
A specialised surface adapted for efficient exchange of substances, such as alveoli, villi or gills.
Breathing movements that move air into and out of the lungs, maintaining concentration gradients.
Surface area divided by volume; it decreases as an organism gets larger.
The overall movement once movement in both directions is taken into account.

mistakes.w: Diffusion is the movement of particles from low to high concentration.
mistakes.r: Net movement from higher to lower concentration, down the concentration gradient.

mistakes.w: Diffusion needs energy.
mistakes.r: Diffusion is passive; it does not need energy from respiration.

mistakes.w: A thicker membrane makes diffusion faster because it is stronger.
mistakes.r: Thicker membrane means greater diffusion distance, so a slower rate (inversely proportional).

mistakes.w: Alveoli have thin walls so oxygen can get through.
mistakes.r: Walls are one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance, so a faster rate of diffusion.

mistakes.w: Good blood supply so oxygen can be carried.
mistakes.r: Good blood supply maintains a steep concentration gradient, so diffusion is faster.

mistakes.w: Fick's law: rate = thickness x area / concentration.
mistakes.r: Rate ∝ (surface area x concentration difference) / thickness of membrane.

mistakes.w: Doubling surface area and doubling thickness doubles the rate.
mistakes.r: The two changes cancel out, so the rate stays the same.

mistakes.w: Emphysema makes alveoli bigger so there is more surface area.
mistakes.r: Fewer, larger air spaces give a smaller total surface area, so the rate of diffusion decreases.

mistakes.w: Particles stop moving when concentrations are equal.
mistakes.r: Particles keep moving randomly; there is just no net movement.

exam.q: State what is meant by diffusion.
model: Net movement of particles
From a higher to a lower concentration / down a concentration gradient
exam.tip: Include the word 'net' for full marks.

exam.q: Write down Fick's law.
model: Rate of diffusion ∝ (surface area x concentration difference) / thickness of membrane
exam.tip: Make sure thickness is on the bottom.

exam.q: Explain how the structure of an alveolus increases the rate of diffusion of oxygen into the blood.
model: Large surface area (many alveoli)
Walls one cell thick / thin so short diffusion distance
Good blood supply / capillary network
Maintains a steep concentration gradient
So oxygen diffuses into the blood faster
exam.tip: Link each feature to a factor in Fick's law.

exam.q: Explain why breathing is needed to maintain a high rate of gas exchange.
model: Brings in fresh air with high oxygen concentration / removes air with high carbon dioxide
Maintains a steep concentration gradient between alveoli and blood
exam.tip: Use the phrase 'maintains a steep concentration gradient'.

exam.q: Calculate the rate of diffusion when surface area = 50 mm², concentration difference = 6 au and membrane thickness = 0.5 mm.
exam.tip: Write the substitution before the answer.

exam.q: A membrane's thickness doubles. State the effect on the rate of diffusion if other factors stay the same.
model: Rate halves
exam.tip: Inverse proportion: double thickness gives half rate.

exam.q: Emphysema destroys the walls between alveoli. Explain why people with emphysema feel tired.
model: Fewer, larger air spaces so smaller surface area
Slower rate of diffusion of oxygen into blood
Less oxygen delivered to cells
Less aerobic respiration so less energy released
exam.tip: Follow the chain all the way to respiration and energy.

exam.q: Suggest why diffusion alone is not enough to supply oxygen to cells in a large organism.
model: Small surface area to volume ratio
Diffusion distance to inner cells is too large / diffusion too slow
exam.tip: Mention both SA:V and distance.

exam.q: Explain how the structure of exchange surfaces in a fish gill and a human small intestine are adapted for efficient diffusion. Use Fick's law in your answer.
model: Fick's law stated: rate ∝ area x concentration difference / thickness
Gills: many filaments and lamellae give a large surface area
Gills: thin lamellae give a short diffusion distance
Gills: good blood supply / countercurrent flow maintains concentration gradient
Small intestine: villi and microvilli give a large surface area
Villi: wall one cell thick gives a short diffusion distance
Villi: rich capillary network carries absorbed food away, maintaining steep gradient
exam.tip: Balance both organs and keep linking to the formula.

exam.q: Give two reasons why the rate of diffusion of oxygen into the blood increases during exercise.
model: Faster/deeper breathing brings more oxygen to the alveoli
Faster blood flow removes oxygenated blood more quickly, so a steeper concentration gradient
exam.tip: Both reasons are about concentration gradient.

worked.q: Exchange surface A has area 120 cm², concentration difference 10 au and thickness 0.2 µm. Surface B has area 60 cm², concentration difference 10 au and thickness 0.05 µm. Which has the faster rate of diffusion, and by what factor?
steps: Fick's law: rate ∝ (surface area x concentration difference) / thickness
worked.ans: Surface B is faster, by a factor of 2, because its much thinner membrane more than makes up for its smaller area.

worked.q: In a lung disease, the total surface area of the alveoli falls to one third of normal and the membrane becomes twice as thick. What fraction of the normal rate of oxygen diffusion remains (concentration difference unchanged)?
steps: Use factors: new rate = old rate x (area factor) / (thickness factor)
Area factor = 1/3
Thickness factor = 2
worked.ans: The rate falls to 1/6 of normal (about 17%), so the person becomes breathless and tired.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why a red blood cell squeezing through a narrow capillary next to an alveolus helps gas exchange.
steps: The red blood cell is pressed against the capillary wall.
This reduces the diffusion distance between the air in the alveolus and the haemoglobin.
Fick's law: rate is inversely proportional to thickness, so a shorter distance gives faster diffusion.
Slow passage also gives more time for oxygen to diffuse in.
worked.ans: Shorter diffusion distance, so a faster rate of oxygen diffusion into the red blood cell.

bio_edx.7.3.summary: Blood is a tissue made of a liquid called plasma in which red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets are suspended. Each component has a structure that suits its function: red blood cells carry oxygen, white blood cells (phagocytes and lymphocytes) defend the body against pathogens, platelets help the blood to clot, and plasma transports dissolved substances, hormones and heat. Edexcel expects you to explain how the structure of each component is related to its function.

core.p: Blood is a **tissue**: a group of cells working together, carried in a liquid. If blood is spun in a centrifuge it separates into layers, which shows its components.
bullets: **Plasma**: about 55% of blood volume, a straw-coloured liquid on top.
**White blood cells and platelets**: a thin pale layer (the buffy coat), less than 1%.
**Red blood cells**: about 45% of blood volume, at the bottom because they are densest.
The four components to learn: **red blood cells (erythrocytes)**, **white blood cells** (**phagocytes** and **lymphocytes**), **platelets** and **plasma**.
Blood is pumped by the heart round the body in blood vessels, linking all the exchange surfaces to all body cells.

callouts.p: Plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells (phagocytes and lymphocytes), platelets.

fig.cap: Blood spun in a centrifuge separates into plasma (about 55%), a thin layer of white blood cells and platelets, and red blood cells (about 45%).

core.p: The job of red blood cells is to **transport oxygen** from the lungs to all respiring cells in the body.
bullets: In the lungs, where oxygen concentration is high, oxygen binds to **haemoglobin** to form **oxyhaemoglobin**.
In tissues, where oxygen concentration is low, oxyhaemoglobin releases oxygen, which diffuses into cells.
Cells use the oxygen for **aerobic respiration**, which releases energy.
Haemoglobin contains **iron**, which is why iron is needed in the diet; a lack causes anaemia (fewer working red cells, tiredness).

callouts.p: Haemoglobin combined with oxygen, formed in the lungs; it releases oxygen in respiring tissues.

core.h: Red blood cells: structure linked to function
core.p: Every feature of a red blood cell helps it carry as much oxygen as possible and exchange it quickly.
bullets: **Biconcave disc** shape: gives a **large surface area to volume ratio**, so oxygen diffuses in and out quickly.
Biconcave shape also gives a **short diffusion distance** to the centre of the cell.
**No nucleus**: leaves more room for haemoglobin, so each cell carries more oxygen.
Packed with **haemoglobin**, the red protein that binds oxygen.
**Small and flexible**: can squeeze through narrow capillaries, close to body cells, so a short diffusion distance to tissues.
Huge numbers: about 5 million per mm³ of blood.

head: Feature
How it helps
rows: Large surface area for fast diffusion of oxygen
More space for haemoglobin, carries more oxygen
Fits through capillaries, close to cells

callouts.t: No nucleus, not no organelles 'for oxygen'
callouts.p: Write 'no nucleus so more room for haemoglobin', not 'no nucleus so more room for oxygen'.

fig.cap: A red blood cell seen from above and in section: the biconcave disc shape gives a large surface area and a short diffusion distance, and there is no nucleus.

core.p: White blood cells are part of the body's **immune system**. They defend the body against **pathogens** (microorganisms that cause disease). Unlike red blood cells, they **have a nucleus**.
bullets: There are fewer white cells than red cells (roughly 1 white cell for every 600-700 red cells).
Edexcel names two types: **phagocytes** and **lymphocytes**.
Their numbers increase during an infection.
They can leave the blood by squeezing through capillary walls to reach infected tissue.

head: Phagocyte
Lymphocyte
rows: Large and round, fills most of cell
Specific: each antibody fits one antigen

core.p: Phagocytes carry out **phagocytosis**: they surround, engulf and digest pathogens. This is a **non-specific** response, so they attack any foreign cell.
bullets: Phagocytes are attracted to the site of infection.
The **flexible cell membrane** and cytoplasm flow around the pathogen to **engulf (ingest)** it.
The pathogen is enclosed in a vacuole inside the phagocyte.
**Enzymes** (e.g. from lysosomes) are released into the vacuole and **digest** the pathogen.
Lobed nucleus helps the phagocyte squeeze through gaps between cells in capillary walls.

callouts.p: The process in which a phagocyte engulfs (ingests) a pathogen and digests it using enzymes.

fig.cap: Phagocytosis: the phagocyte moves towards the pathogen, engulfs it with its flexible membrane, then digests it with enzymes inside a vacuole.

core.p: Lymphocytes **produce antibodies**. This is a **specific** response: each type of antibody fits only one type of **antigen**.
bullets: **Antigens** are molecules (usually proteins) on the surface of pathogens.
A lymphocyte with the matching receptor is activated and divides to make many copies.
These produce large amounts of the **specific antibody** that is complementary in shape to the antigen.
Antibodies bind to antigens, making pathogens clump together (easier for phagocytes to engulf) or marking them for destruction.
Some lymphocytes produce **antitoxins** that neutralise toxins made by bacteria.
Some become **memory lymphocytes**, so a second infection by the same pathogen triggers a faster, larger response (this is how immunity and vaccination work).
Large nucleus and lots of protein-making machinery (ribosomes), because antibodies are proteins.

callouts.p: A protein made by lymphocytes that binds to a specific antigen on a pathogen.
Phagocytes engulf. Lymphocytes make antibodies. Do not mix them up.

core.p: Platelets are **small fragments of cells** with **no nucleus**. Their function is to help the blood to **clot** at a wound.
bullets: When a blood vessel is damaged, platelets stick to the damaged area and to each other.
They release chemicals that trigger a series of reactions in the plasma.
This converts the soluble plasma protein fibrinogen into insoluble **fibrin** threads.
The fibrin forms a **mesh** that traps red blood cells and platelets, forming a **clot**.
The clot dries to a **scab**.
Why clotting matters: it **stops blood loss** and **prevents pathogens entering** the body through the wound.

callouts.p: Stops excessive bleeding and stops microorganisms getting in.

core.p: Plasma is the **liquid** part of blood, about 90% water. It **transports** substances dissolved in it around the body and carries the blood cells.
bullets: **Carbon dioxide** from respiring cells to the lungs (mostly as hydrogencarbonate ions).
**Digested food** such as glucose and amino acids from the small intestine to cells.
**Urea** from the liver to the kidneys for excretion.
**Hormones** from endocrine glands to target organs (e.g. insulin, adrenaline).
**Proteins** such as antibodies and clotting proteins (fibrinogen).
**Heat** (thermal energy) from active organs such as muscles and the liver, spreading it round the body.
**Mineral ions** and water.

callouts.t: Oxygen is not carried by plasma
callouts.p: Almost all oxygen is carried by haemoglobin in red blood cells, not dissolved in plasma.

core.p: Comparison tables are popular in exams. Notice which components have a nucleus and how numbers compare.
bullets: Only white blood cells have a nucleus.
Red blood cells are by far the most numerous.
Platelets are the smallest and are only fragments of cells.
All components are made in the **bone marrow**.

core.p: You may be shown a blood smear (micrograph) and asked to identify the components.
bullets: Red blood cells: many, pale in the centre (because of the biconcave shape), no nucleus.
Phagocyte: larger, with a **lobed** nucleus that stains dark.
Lymphocyte: about the size of a red cell or slightly larger, with a **large round nucleus** filling most of the cell and a thin rim of cytoplasm.
Platelets: tiny dark specks between the cells.

callouts.p: Lobed nucleus = phagocyte. Big round nucleus = lymphocyte. No nucleus = red cell or platelet.

core.p: Applying knowledge of blood components lets you explain symptoms in unfamiliar contexts.
bullets: Fewer red blood cells or less haemoglobin (**anaemia**): less oxygen carried, so less aerobic respiration, tiredness and breathlessness.
Low white cell count: more infections because fewer pathogens are destroyed.
Low platelet count: bruises easily and wounds bleed for longer.
High altitude: the body makes more red blood cells over time to carry more oxygen, which is why athletes train at altitude.
Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen, so less oxygen is carried.

core.p: Most questions on this point ask you to link a structure to a function. Always give the feature and then explain the benefit.
bullets: Use the chain: feature, so effect, so benefit.
Example: 'No nucleus, so more space for haemoglobin, so more oxygen can be carried.'
Use correct names: **haemoglobin**, **oxyhaemoglobin**, **phagocytosis**, **antibodies**, **antigens**, **fibrin**.
For 6-mark questions, cover all four components with a structure and function for each.

callouts.p: Haemoglobin, not haemogoblin. Phagocyte, not fagocyte.

analogy.t: Blood as a city's delivery and security network
analogy.p: Plasma is the river that everything floats along. Red blood cells are delivery lorries built only to carry one cargo (oxygen), with the driver's cab removed (no nucleus) to fit more crates (haemoglobin). Phagocytes are security guards who grab and destroy any intruder. Lymphocytes are a lab that makes custom-made handcuffs (antibodies) that fit only one type of criminal. Platelets are emergency repair crews who patch holes in the pipes. Where it breaks down: lorries choose where to go, but red cells are carried passively by the flow; and lymphocytes do not design antibodies on purpose, the right lymphocyte is selected and copied.

terms.d: The liquid part of blood, mostly water, which transports dissolved substances, hormones, proteins and heat.
Biconcave cell with no nucleus, containing haemoglobin, that carries oxygen.
Red, iron-containing protein in red blood cells that binds oxygen.
Haemoglobin combined with oxygen.
Disc shape that is thinner in the middle than at the edge on both sides.
Blood cell with a nucleus that defends the body against pathogens.
White blood cell that engulfs and digests pathogens.
Engulfing and digesting a pathogen.
White blood cell that produces antibodies.
Protein produced by lymphocytes that binds to a specific antigen.
Molecule on the surface of a pathogen that is recognised by antibodies.
Substance produced by lymphocytes that neutralises a toxin.
Small cell fragment with no nucleus that helps the blood clot.
Insoluble protein threads that form a mesh in a blood clot.
A microorganism that causes disease.
Mesh of fibrin, platelets and trapped red cells that seals a wound.

mistakes.w: Red blood cells have no nucleus so there is more room for oxygen.
mistakes.r: No nucleus so more room for haemoglobin, so more oxygen can be carried.

mistakes.w: Biconcave shape lets them fit through capillaries.
mistakes.r: Biconcave shape gives a large surface area (to volume ratio) for faster diffusion of oxygen.

mistakes.w: Lymphocytes eat bacteria.
mistakes.r: Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens; lymphocytes produce antibodies.

mistakes.w: White blood cells kill viruses by making antibiotics.
mistakes.r: Lymphocytes produce antibodies (and antitoxins); antibiotics are medicines.

mistakes.w: Platelets are small cells.
mistakes.r: Platelets are fragments of cells with no nucleus.

mistakes.w: Plasma carries oxygen.
mistakes.r: Oxygen is carried by haemoglobin in red blood cells; plasma carries CO2, glucose, urea, hormones, proteins and heat.

mistakes.w: Clotting stops germs.
mistakes.r: Clotting prevents blood loss and prevents pathogens entering through the wound.

mistakes.w: Antibodies attack any pathogen.
mistakes.r: Antibodies are specific: each binds to one complementary antigen.

exam.q: Name the component of the blood that helps blood to clot.
model: Platelets
exam.tip: One word answer is enough.

exam.q: Give two substances transported by plasma.
model: Any two from: carbon dioxide, glucose, amino acids, urea, hormones, proteins/antibodies, mineral ions, heat
exam.tip: Do not write oxygen.

exam.q: Explain how two features of a red blood cell adapt it for its function.
model: Biconcave shape
Gives large surface area for diffusion of oxygen
No nucleus
More room for haemoglobin so carries more oxygen
exam.tip: Feature then explanation, twice.

exam.q: Describe how a phagocyte destroys a pathogen.

Digests it using enzymes

Prevents entry of pathogens / microorganisms
exam.tip: Two separate reasons.

Less energy released

Phagocytes: flexible membrane to engulf pathogens, enzymes digest them

With fewer platelets, less fibrin mesh forms at wounds, so cuts bleed for longer and the person bruises easily.

bio_edx.7.4.summary: Blood travels round the body in three main types of blood vessel: arteries, veins and capillaries. Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure, so they have thick muscular and elastic walls; veins carry blood back to the heart at low pressure, so they have thin walls, a wide lumen and valves to stop backflow; capillaries link the two and have walls only one cell thick so substances can diffuse quickly between the blood and the cells. Edexcel expects you to explain how the structure of each vessel is related to its function.

core.h: The three types of blood vessel
core.p: The heart pumps blood into **arteries**, which branch into smaller arterioles and then into **capillaries** in the tissues. Capillaries join up into venules and then **veins**, which carry blood back to the heart.
bullets: **Arteries** carry blood **away from the heart**.
**Veins** carry blood **towards the heart**.
**Capillaries** connect arteries and veins and are the site of **exchange** with body cells.
The **lumen** is the hollow centre of a vessel that blood flows through.
Blood pressure is highest in arteries, falls in capillaries and is lowest in veins.

callouts.p: Arteries carry blood Away from the heart. Veins carry blood into the heart.

fig.cap: The route of blood: the heart pumps blood into arteries, which branch into capillaries in the tissues; capillaries join to form veins, which return blood to the heart.

core.p: Arteries carry blood **away from the heart** to the organs. Because the ventricles contract forcefully, the blood in arteries is at **high pressure** and flows in surges (the pulse).
bullets: Most arteries carry **oxygenated** blood.
Exception: the **pulmonary artery** carries **deoxygenated** blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
The **aorta** is the largest artery, carrying oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body.
You can feel your **pulse** where an artery passes near the skin, e.g. the wrist (radial artery) or neck.

callouts.t: Not all arteries carry oxygenated blood
callouts.p: Define arteries by direction (away from the heart), not by oxygen content.

core.p: Every feature of an artery helps it cope with high-pressure blood surging out of the heart.
bullets: **Thick walls**: withstand the **high pressure** without bursting.
**Thick layer of muscle**: can contract to help control blood flow (narrowing or widening the vessel).
**Thick layer of elastic fibres**: the wall **stretches** as each surge of blood arrives and **recoils** (springs back) between beats, which **evens out the flow** and keeps pressure up.
**Narrow lumen** compared to wall thickness: helps maintain high pressure.
**No valves** (except at the base of the aorta and pulmonary artery as they leave the heart), because high pressure keeps blood moving forward.

callouts.p: Elastic fibres stretch and recoil, smoothing the flow from surges into a more even flow and maintaining pressure.

core.p: Veins carry blood **towards the heart**. By the time blood reaches the veins it has passed through capillaries, so it is at **low pressure** and flows slowly and steadily.
bullets: Most veins carry **deoxygenated** blood.
Exception: the **pulmonary vein** carries **oxygenated** blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
The **vena cava** is the largest vein, returning deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium.
Veins hold a large proportion of the body's blood at any one time.

core.p: Because the pressure is low, veins do not need thick walls. Their main problem is keeping blood moving in the right direction.
bullets: **Thin walls** with **less muscle and elastic tissue**: no need to withstand high pressure.
**Large (wide) lumen**: lowers resistance to flow, so low-pressure blood can still flow easily.
**Valves**: flaps that close if blood starts to flow backwards, **preventing backflow** and keeping blood flowing towards the heart.
Many veins run between **skeletal muscles**; when muscles contract they squeeze the vein and push blood along, and the valves make sure it only goes towards the heart.
This is why standing still for a long time can make blood pool in the legs.

callouts.p: Prevent the backflow of blood, so blood flows only towards the heart.

fig.cap: Valves in a vein: when blood flows towards the heart the valve opens; if blood starts to flow backwards the valve flaps fill and close, preventing backflow.

core.p: Capillaries are where **exchange** happens between the blood and the body cells. They form dense networks called **capillary beds** in every tissue.
bullets: **Oxygen** and **glucose** diffuse out of the blood into cells for respiration.
**Carbon dioxide** and other waste such as **urea** diffuse from cells into the blood.
Some plasma is pushed out to form **tissue fluid**, which bathes the cells.
In the lungs, capillaries around the alveoli pick up oxygen and lose carbon dioxide.

core.p: Capillaries are built for fast diffusion. Their features match the factors in Fick's law.
bullets: Walls **one cell thick**: very **short diffusion distance**, so substances diffuse quickly.
Some capillaries have small gaps (are **permeable**), letting plasma leak out to form tissue fluid.
**Very narrow lumen**, only about as wide as a red blood cell: red cells pass in single file, close to the wall, which shortens the diffusion distance.
**Huge numbers** forming **large networks**: large surface area, and every cell is close to a capillary.
Blood flows **slowly** through capillaries, giving more time for exchange.
No muscle or elastic layer, because pressure is low and they need to be thin.

callouts.p: Capillary walls are one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance for fast exchange.

fig.cap: Exchange at a capillary: the wall is one cell thick, so oxygen and glucose diffuse quickly into body cells while carbon dioxide diffuses into the blood.

bullets: Wall thickness: artery > vein > capillary.
Lumen size: vein > artery > capillary.
Only veins have valves along their length.
Pressure: artery > capillary > vein.

core.p: Blood pressure falls as blood moves away from the heart. Understanding why helps explain vessel structure.
bullets: Pressure is **highest in the aorta and arteries** and rises and falls with each heartbeat.
Elastic recoil of artery walls keeps pressure from falling to zero between beats.
Pressure **drops a lot in arterioles and capillaries** because the many narrow vessels create resistance.
Pressure is **lowest in the veins**, which is why veins need valves and help from muscles.
Blood flows **slowest in capillaries** because their total cross-sectional area is very large.

callouts.p: Big fluctuating line = arteries. Steep fall = arterioles and capillaries. Low flat line = veins.

core.h: Identifying vessels from data or images
core.p: Exam questions often show a micrograph or give measurements and ask you to identify the vessel.
bullets: Thick wall relative to lumen, and round shape: **artery**.
Thin wall, large lumen, often squashed or irregular shape, may show valves: **vein**.
Tiny vessel with a wall one cell thick, about 5-10 µm across: **capillary**.
A useful calculation: ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter is much higher for an artery than for a vein.

callouts.t: Do not say veins have no muscle
callouts.p: Veins do have muscle and elastic tissue, just thinner layers than arteries.

core.h: Applying the ideas: health and disease
core.p: Knowing vessel structure lets you explain problems in unfamiliar contexts.
bullets: **Coronary heart disease**: fatty deposits narrow the lumen of coronary arteries, reducing blood flow and oxygen to heart muscle.
Loss of elasticity in arteries with age makes them less able to stretch, raising blood pressure.
**Varicose veins**: valves become weak and leak, so blood pools and veins swell.
Walking or moving the legs on long flights uses muscles to squeeze veins and stops blood pooling.
A cut artery spurts blood (high pressure, pulse); a cut vein oozes steadily (low pressure).

core.p: Answer structure-function questions with a clear link each time: feature, then why it helps.
bullets: Artery example: 'Thick muscular and elastic wall, to withstand high pressure and stretch and recoil to maintain pressure.'
Vein example: 'Valves to prevent backflow of blood.'
Capillary example: 'Wall one cell thick, so short diffusion distance for fast exchange.'
For comparison questions, use comparative words: thicker, thinner, wider, narrower.
For 6-mark questions, cover all three vessels with at least two linked features each.

callouts.p: A list of features without reasons usually scores only half the marks.

analogy.p: Arteries are high-pressure water mains: thick, strong pipes that bulge slightly with every pump surge and spring back. Capillaries are the tiny leaky garden hoses running past every plant, where water actually gets out to where it is needed. Veins are wide, low-pressure drains back to the pumping station, with one-way flaps so water cannot flow back down hill. Where it breaks down: water pipes are rigid and do not contract, whereas artery walls contain living muscle that can change their width, and real drains rely on gravity, not on squeezing by surrounding muscles.

terms.d: Blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart at high pressure.
Blood vessel that carries blood towards the heart at low pressure.
Tiny blood vessel with a wall one cell thick where substances are exchanged with cells.
The hollow space inside a blood vessel through which blood flows.
Tissue in vessel walls that stretches and recoils, smoothing blood flow and maintaining pressure.
Flap of tissue in veins (and the heart) that prevents backflow of blood.
Blood flowing in the wrong direction, away from the heart in veins.
Largest artery, carrying oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body.
Largest vein, returning deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium.
Artery carrying deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs.
Vein carrying oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart.
Network of capillaries in a tissue.
Fluid that leaks out of capillaries and bathes the cells.
Surge of pressure in an artery caused by each contraction of the ventricles.
Distance a substance must travel; very short across a capillary wall.

mistakes.w: Arteries carry oxygenated blood and veins carry deoxygenated blood.
mistakes.r: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins towards it; the pulmonary artery and vein are exceptions to the oxygen rule.

mistakes.w: Arteries have thick walls to pump blood.
mistakes.r: Thick walls withstand high pressure; the heart pumps blood, not the arteries.

mistakes.w: Veins have valves to pump blood to the heart.
mistakes.r: Valves prevent backflow of blood.

mistakes.w: Capillaries have thin walls so blood can get out.
mistakes.r: Walls one cell thick give a short diffusion distance so substances diffuse quickly between blood and cells.

mistakes.w: Arteries have a large lumen.
mistakes.r: Arteries have a narrow lumen relative to their thick wall; veins have a large lumen.

mistakes.w: Elastic walls let arteries expand to hold more blood.
mistakes.r: Elastic fibres stretch and recoil to withstand surges and even out the flow, maintaining pressure.

mistakes.w: Veins have no muscle.
mistakes.r: Veins have thinner layers of muscle and elastic tissue than arteries.

mistakes.w: Blood cells leave capillaries to feed cells.
mistakes.r: Substances such as oxygen and glucose diffuse out; red blood cells stay inside the capillary.

exam.q: Name the type of blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart.
model: Artery
exam.tip: Remember A for Away.

exam.q: State the function of valves in veins.
model: Prevent backflow of blood
exam.tip: Use the word 'backflow'.

exam.q: Explain why the walls of arteries are thick and contain elastic fibres.
model: Blood in arteries is at high pressure
Thick wall withstands the high pressure
Elastic fibres stretch and recoil to even out flow / maintain pressure
exam.tip: Link structure to pressure.

exam.q: Explain how capillaries are adapted for the exchange of substances.
model: Wall one cell thick
Short diffusion distance
Large network / large surface area / close to every cell
exam.tip: Always say 'one cell thick'.

exam.q: Give two differences between the structure of an artery and a vein.
model: Artery has a thicker wall / more muscle and elastic tissue
Vein has a larger lumen
Vein has valves; artery does not
exam.tip: Use comparatives in each point.

exam.q: Explain why veins have a large lumen.
model: Blood in veins is at low pressure
Large lumen reduces resistance so blood flows easily back to the heart
exam.tip: Mention low pressure.

exam.q: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood. Explain why it is still called an artery.
model: It carries blood away from the heart
Arteries are defined by direction of flow / it has the structure of an artery
exam.tip: Direction, not oxygen content.

exam.q: Explain why blood flows slowly through capillaries and why this is an advantage.
model: Low pressure / large total cross-sectional area / narrow lumen
More time for diffusion / exchange of substances
exam.tip: Give both the reason and the benefit.

exam.q: Compare the structure of arteries, veins and capillaries and explain how each is related to its function.
model: Arteries carry blood away from heart at high pressure
Arteries: thick muscular wall withstands pressure; elastic fibres stretch and recoil
Veins carry blood to the heart at low pressure
Veins: thin wall and large lumen; valves prevent backflow
Capillaries exchange substances with cells
Capillaries: wall one cell thick for short diffusion distance; large network, narrow lumen
exam.tip: Treat all three vessels equally and link every feature to its purpose.

exam.q: A person stands still for a long time and their ankles swell. Suggest why moving the legs helps prevent this.
model: Contracting leg muscles squeeze the veins
Pushes blood towards the heart; valves prevent backflow so blood does not pool
exam.tip: Link muscles and valves together.

worked.q: In a micrograph, vessel X has a wall thickness of 0.9 mm and lumen diameter of 1.5 mm. Vessel Y has wall thickness 0.3 mm and lumen diameter 3.0 mm. Calculate the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter for each and identify which is the artery.
steps: X has a much thicker wall relative to its lumen.
Arteries have thick walls and narrow lumens; veins have thin walls and wide lumens.
worked.ans: X (ratio 0.6) is the artery; Y (ratio 0.1) is the vein.

worked.q: A capillary has a lumen diameter of 8 µm. A red blood cell has a diameter of 7.5 µm. Explain why this is an advantage for oxygen delivery.
steps: The lumen is only just wider than a red blood cell.
Red blood cells pass through in single file, pressed close to the capillary wall.
This makes the diffusion distance from haemoglobin to the tissue very short.
The cells also move slowly, giving more time for diffusion.
worked.ans: Short diffusion distance and more time, so oxygen diffuses into the cells quickly.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why a cut artery spurts blood but a cut vein oozes.
steps: Blood in arteries is at high pressure, coming straight from the heart.
The pressure rises and falls with each heartbeat (pulse), so blood spurts in time with the heartbeat.
Blood in veins has passed through capillaries, where pressure falls a lot.
Low pressure means blood flows out of a vein slowly and steadily.
worked.ans: Arteries carry high, pulsing pressure so blood spurts; veins have low, steady pressure so blood oozes.

bio_edx.7.5.summary: The human heart is a **double pump** made of cardiac muscle that keeps blood moving round a **double circulatory system**: the right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs and the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. Every structure links to a job: **valves** stop backflow, the **septum** keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood apart, and the **thickness of each chamber wall** matches how far and how hard that chamber must push blood. Learn the four chambers, the four major blood vessels and the route blood takes, and always explain structure using the word **because**.

core.h: Why we need a heart and a circulatory system
core.p: Humans are large, multicellular organisms with a **small surface area to volume ratio**, so diffusion alone is far too slow to get oxygen and glucose to every cell or to remove carbon dioxide and urea. The circulatory system is a **mass transport system**: the heart pumps blood through a network of blood vessels so that substances are carried quickly over long distances, then exchanged by diffusion across capillary walls.
bullets: The circulatory system is made of the **heart**, the **blood vessels** (arteries, veins, capillaries) and the **blood**.
Blood **delivers** oxygen (from the lungs) and glucose and other nutrients (from the small intestine) to respiring cells.
Blood **removes** waste: carbon dioxide (to the lungs) and urea (to the kidneys).
The heart provides the **pressure** that drives blood flow; without it blood would not move through the vessels.
The heart is an **organ** made mainly of **cardiac muscle** tissue, which contracts rhythmically without tiring.

callouts.p: Almost every exam question on this point is really asking: name the structure, then say **what it does** and **why its structure helps it do that**.

core.h: The four chambers of the heart
core.p: The heart has **four chambers**. The two upper chambers are the **atria** (singular atrium) which receive blood from veins. The two lower chambers are the **ventricles** which pump blood out into arteries. Each side of the heart has one atrium and one ventricle.
bullets: **Right atrium**: receives **deoxygenated** blood from the body through the **vena cava**.
**Right ventricle**: pumps deoxygenated blood to the **lungs** through the **pulmonary artery**.
**Left atrium**: receives **oxygenated** blood from the lungs through the **pulmonary vein**.
**Left ventricle**: pumps oxygenated blood to the **whole body** through the **aorta**.
Atria contract first to push blood down into the ventricles; then the ventricles contract to push blood out of the heart.
Both sides of the heart contract at the same time, so the same volume of blood leaves each ventricle with every beat.

callouts.t: Left and right are swapped on diagrams
callouts.p: Heart diagrams are drawn as if you are **facing the person**, so the **left side of the heart appears on the right of the page**. Find the thick-walled ventricle or the aorta to work out which side is which.

core.p: Four major blood vessels connect to the heart. A simple rule: **arteries carry blood away from the heart** and **veins carry blood into the heart**. The pulmonary vessels are the only exceptions to the usual pattern of arteries carrying oxygenated blood.
bullets: **Vena cava** (a vein): brings **deoxygenated** blood from the body back to the **right atrium**.
**Pulmonary artery**: takes **deoxygenated** blood from the **right ventricle** to the **lungs**. It is the only artery carrying deoxygenated blood.
**Pulmonary vein**: brings **oxygenated** blood from the lungs to the **left atrium**. It is the only vein carrying oxygenated blood.
**Aorta**: the largest artery; carries **oxygenated** blood at **high pressure** from the **left ventricle** to the body.
**Coronary arteries** branch off the aorta and run over the surface of the heart, supplying the heart muscle itself with oxygen and glucose for respiration.
Pulmonary means 'to do with the lungs', which helps you remember where these vessels go.

callouts.p: **A**rteries carry blood **A**way from the heart. Use this, not oxygen content, to decide whether a vessel is an artery or a vein.

core.h: The route of blood through the heart
core.p: Being able to put the structures in the correct order is one of the most commonly tested skills. Blood passes through the heart **twice** on one complete trip round the body.
bullets: Body → **vena cava** → **right atrium** → valve → **right ventricle** → semilunar valve → **pulmonary artery** → **lungs**.
In the lungs blood picks up **oxygen** and gives up **carbon dioxide** by diffusion in the capillaries around the alveoli.
Lungs → **pulmonary vein** → **left atrium** → valve → **left ventricle** → semilunar valve → **aorta** → **body**.
In body tissues blood gives up oxygen and glucose to respiring cells and picks up carbon dioxide, so it returns deoxygenated.
Blood always enters a heart side through an **atrium** and leaves through a **ventricle**.

callouts.p: In a 'describe the pathway of blood' question name **every** chamber, valve and vessel in order, and say where the blood becomes oxygenated (lungs) and deoxygenated (body tissues).

core.p: Humans have a **double circulatory system**: blood passes through the heart **twice** for every complete circuit of the body. There are two separate loops, both driven by the same heart.
bullets: **Pulmonary circulation**: right ventricle → lungs → left atrium. It picks up oxygen and removes carbon dioxide.
**Systemic circulation**: left ventricle → body organs → right atrium. It delivers oxygen and glucose and collects waste.
After blood passes through the lung capillaries its pressure falls a lot; returning it to the heart lets the left ventricle **re-pressurise** it before it goes to the body.
So blood reaches the body tissues at **high pressure**, which means it flows **faster** and delivers oxygen and glucose more quickly, supporting a high rate of respiration.
Blood to the lungs is kept at **lower pressure**, which protects the delicate lung capillaries from damage and gives time for gas exchange.
This matters for mammals and birds which have a **high metabolic rate** and need a fast supply of oxygen for respiration, partly to release energy to keep their body temperature constant.
Fish have a **single circulatory system** (heart → gills → body → heart), so blood reaches the body at lower pressure.

callouts.p: A circulatory system in which blood passes through the heart **twice** for every complete circuit of the body: once through the pulmonary circuit to the lungs and once through the systemic circuit to the rest of the body.
