core.p: **Valves** make sure blood flows in **one direction only** through the heart. They are flaps of tough tissue that are pushed open by blood flowing forwards and are forced shut when blood tries to flow backwards. **Tendons** (sometimes called valve tendons or chordae tendineae) anchor the valves between the atria and ventricles so they cannot turn inside out.
bullets: **Atrioventricular valves** lie between each atrium and ventricle. On the right it is the **tricuspid valve**; on the left it is the **bicuspid (mitral) valve**.
When the ventricles contract, pressure in the ventricle rises above the atrium, **closing** the atrioventricular valve so blood cannot go back into the atrium.
**Semilunar valves** lie at the base of the **pulmonary artery** and the **aorta**.
When the ventricles relax, pressure in the ventricle falls below the artery, so blood tries to flow back; this **closes** the semilunar valve.
Valves open and close because of **pressure differences**, not because muscles pull them.
The 'lub-dub' sound of the heartbeat is the sound of valves closing.
If a valve is faulty (leaky) some blood flows backwards, so less blood is pumped forward each beat and the heart must work harder.

callouts.p: Writing 'valves control blood' gets no marks. The mark scheme wants: valves **prevent the backflow of blood** / keep blood flowing in **one direction**.

core.h: Relative thickness of the chamber walls
core.p: The walls of the chambers are made of cardiac muscle. The **thicker** the muscle, the **more forcefully** it can contract and the **higher the pressure** it produces. Each wall is only as thick as its job needs.
bullets: **Atria have thin walls** because they only need to push blood a short distance down into the ventricles, helped by gravity.
**Ventricles have thicker walls** than atria because they pump blood out of the heart into arteries, which needs much more force.

The **left ventricle wall is the thickest** (about three times thicker than the right) because it must pump blood at **high pressure** all round the **whole body**, a long distance with lots of resistance.
The **right ventricle wall is thinner** because it only pumps blood a short distance to the **lungs**, and a lower pressure is needed so the delicate capillaries in the lungs are not damaged.
Both ventricles hold and pump the **same volume** of blood; the difference is the **pressure**, not the amount.

callouts.p: A common higher-level point: the left ventricle does **not** pump more blood than the right. It pumps the **same volume at a higher pressure**.

core.p: The **septum** is a thick wall of muscle and tissue that divides the heart into a left side and a right side.
bullets: It **separates oxygenated blood** (left side) from **deoxygenated blood** (right side) so they cannot mix.
If they mixed, blood reaching the body would carry **less oxygen**, so cells would get less oxygen for aerobic respiration.
Keeping them apart maintains a **steep concentration gradient** of oxygen between blood and cells, so oxygen diffuses into tissues quickly.
A 'hole in the heart' is a gap in the septum; babies born with one may look bluish and get tired easily because their blood is less oxygenated.

callouts.p: The wall of tissue dividing the left and right sides of the heart, which **prevents oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from mixing**.

core.h: Cardiac muscle and the coronary arteries
core.p: The heart is made of **cardiac muscle**, a special muscle tissue that contracts and relaxes continuously throughout life without getting tired. Like all muscle, it needs a constant supply of oxygen and glucose for **aerobic respiration** to release the energy needed for contraction.
bullets: Cardiac muscle cells contain **many mitochondria** to carry out lots of aerobic respiration.
The heart cannot use the blood inside its chambers for its own supply because the walls are too thick for diffusion to reach all the cells.
Instead the **coronary arteries** branch from the aorta and spread over the heart surface, carrying oxygenated blood to the heart muscle.
If a coronary artery becomes blocked (for example by fatty deposits), part of the heart muscle is starved of oxygen and can die, causing a **heart attack**.

callouts.p: Questions often ask why the heart muscle needs its own blood supply. Answer: to supply **oxygen and glucose** for **aerobic respiration** to release **energy** for **contraction**.

core.h: Arteries and veins at the heart: pressure link
core.p: The vessels attached to the heart reflect the pressure of the blood they carry. Details of vessel structure belong to the arteries, veins and capillaries spec point, but you should link the major vessels to the chambers they join.
bullets: The **aorta** receives blood at the highest pressure in the body because it is joined to the left ventricle, the thickest-walled chamber.
The **pulmonary artery** carries blood at a lower pressure than the aorta because the right ventricle is less muscular.
The **vena cava** and **pulmonary vein** carry blood at low pressure because the blood has already passed through capillaries, where pressure drops.
Low-pressure blood flows into the atria, which have thin walls that can stretch easily as they fill.

core.h: How structure links to function: summary
core.p: Use this as a checklist for any 'explain how the structure of the heart is related to its function' question.
bullets: **Four chambers** in two sides: lets the heart act as **two pumps** in one, serving the double circulation.
**Thick muscular walls** of cardiac muscle: contract strongly to create pressure to pump blood.
**Left ventricle thickest**: highest pressure to push blood round the whole body.
**Thin atrial walls**: only need to push blood into the ventricles.
**Valves**: prevent backflow so blood flows one way.
**Septum**: stops oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mixing.
**Coronary arteries**: supply heart muscle with oxygen and glucose for respiration.
**Double circulation**: high pressure to the body for fast delivery, lower pressure to the lungs to protect capillaries.

callouts.p: For each structure, write the feature, then **because**, then the function. Feature with no reason usually scores only half the marks.

analogy.t: The heart as a two-pump water park
analogy.p: Imagine a water park with two pumps side by side in one pump house. The small right pump only lifts water to a nearby splash pool (the lungs), so it is small and gentle so it does not break the delicate pool. The big left pump has to push water up the giant slide that winds round the whole park (the body), so it has a much more powerful motor (the thick left ventricle). One-way flap gates (valves) stop water sliding back into the pumps, and a solid wall (the septum) keeps the clean and used water apart. Where it breaks down: in a water park the water is pumped round one circuit after the other, but in the heart both pumps contract at the same time, and the 'water' (blood) is changed chemically as it gains and loses oxygen.

terms.d: An upper, thin-walled chamber of the heart that receives blood from veins and pumps it into the ventricle below.
A lower, thick-walled chamber of the heart that pumps blood out of the heart into an artery.
The wall dividing the left and right sides of the heart, preventing oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mixing.
A flap of tissue that closes when blood tries to flow backwards, so blood flows in one direction only.
A valve between an atrium and a ventricle (tricuspid on the right, bicuspid on the left).
A valve at the base of the aorta or pulmonary artery that prevents blood flowing back into the ventricle.
The large vein that returns deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium.
The artery that carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
The vein that carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
The largest artery, carrying oxygenated blood at high pressure from the left ventricle to the body.
Arteries branching from the aorta that supply the heart muscle with oxygenated blood.
The muscle tissue of the heart, which contracts rhythmically and continuously without fatigue.
A system where blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit of the body.
The circuit carrying blood from the right ventricle to the lungs and back to the left atrium.
The circuit carrying blood from the left ventricle to the body organs and back to the right atrium.
Blood with a high concentration of oxygen, having passed through the lungs.
Blood with a low concentration of oxygen, having given up oxygen to respiring body cells.

mistakes.r: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry blood towards it; the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.

So blood pumped to the body carries less oxygen

worked.q: A student says: 'The right ventricle must pump less blood than the left ventricle because its wall is thinner.' Evaluate this statement.
steps: Identify the claim: thinner wall means less blood pumped.
Recall: both ventricles contract at the same time and pump the same volume of blood per beat, otherwise blood would build up in one circuit.
Explain the real reason for the difference: wall thickness affects the force of contraction and so the pressure produced.
The right ventricle pumps to the nearby lungs, where low pressure is needed to protect capillaries; the left pumps round the whole body, so needs higher pressure.
worked.ans: The statement is incorrect: both ventricles pump the same volume of blood, but the left has a thicker muscular wall so it can produce a higher pressure to pump blood round the whole body, while the right needs only low pressure to send blood to the lungs.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why a faulty semilunar valve in the aorta would make a person breathless during exercise.
steps: State the normal function: the semilunar valve closes when the ventricle relaxes, preventing blood flowing back from the aorta into the left ventricle.
If faulty, some blood flows back into the left ventricle after each beat.
So less oxygenated blood reaches the body per beat.
Muscles receive less oxygen for aerobic respiration during exercise, so more anaerobic respiration happens and the person breathes harder to try to get more oxygen.
worked.ans: Backflow of blood into the left ventricle reduces the volume of oxygenated blood delivered to muscles, so less oxygen is available for aerobic respiration and the person becomes breathless.

bio_edx.7.6.summary: **Cellular respiration** is a series of enzyme-controlled reactions that happens **continuously** in every living cell to release energy from glucose for metabolic processes. Because it releases energy (some as heat) to the surroundings it is an **exothermic** reaction. **Aerobic respiration** uses oxygen, happens mainly in the mitochondria, breaks glucose down completely to carbon dioxide and water, and releases a lot of energy; **anaerobic respiration** happens without oxygen in the cytoplasm, breaks glucose down only partly (to lactic acid in animals, or ethanol and carbon dioxide in plants and yeast) and releases much less energy.

core.p: Respiration is a **chemical process** that happens inside cells. It is **not** the same as breathing. Breathing (ventilation) moves air in and out of the lungs; respiration is the reactions inside cells that release energy from glucose. Respiration is controlled by **enzymes**, so its rate depends on temperature and pH.
bullets: It happens in **every living cell** of every organism: animals, plants, fungi and microorganisms.
It happens **continuously**, day and night, because cells always need energy to stay alive.
The main substrate is **glucose**, which comes from digested food in animals or from photosynthesis in plants.
There are two types: **aerobic** (with oxygen) and **anaerobic** (without oxygen).
Plants respire all the time too, even in the light while they photosynthesise.

callouts.p: An **exothermic** reaction that occurs **continuously** in living cells to **release energy** from glucose for **metabolic processes**.
Energy cannot be made or destroyed. Write that respiration **releases** or **transfers** energy. 'Produces energy' or 'makes energy' loses the mark.

core.p: An **exothermic reaction** transfers energy **to the surroundings**. In respiration, the chemical energy stored in glucose is greater than the energy stored in the products. The difference is released: some is used by the cell for its metabolic processes and some is lost as **heat**, which warms the cell and its surroundings.
bullets: The reactants (glucose and oxygen) store **more chemical energy** than the products (carbon dioxide and water).
So overall energy is **released** during the reaction, which is the definition of exothermic.
The heat released is why your body warms up during exercise, when the rate of respiration increases.
Germinating seeds in a vacuum flask become warmer than boiled (dead) seeds because the living seeds are respiring and releasing heat.
Respiration releases energy in **small steps**, each controlled by an enzyme, rather than all at once like burning; this lets cells capture the energy usefully.

callouts.p: Respiration is exothermic because it **transfers energy from glucose to the surroundings**; the products have less stored energy than the reactants.

core.h: What the energy is used for: metabolic processes
core.p: The energy released by respiration is used to drive the **metabolic processes** that keep the organism alive. Metabolism is the sum of all the reactions in a cell or organism. These processes need a constant energy supply, which is why respiration must happen continuously.
bullets: **Muscle contraction**, so animals can move and the heart can beat.
**Active transport**, moving substances against a concentration gradient (for example mineral ions into root hair cells, or glucose absorbed in the small intestine).
**Synthesis of large molecules** from smaller ones: proteins from amino acids, starch, glycogen and cellulose from glucose, and lipids from fatty acids and glycerol.
**Keeping body temperature constant** in mammals and birds, using the heat released.
**Cell division** and growth, and transmitting **nerve impulses**.

callouts.p: A common question is 'give three uses of the energy released in respiration'. Safe answers: **muscle contraction**, **active transport**, **making large molecules such as proteins**, **keeping warm**.

core.p: **Aerobic respiration** is respiration **using oxygen**. Glucose is broken down **completely** to carbon dioxide and water, so **a large amount of energy** is released from each glucose molecule. Most of the reactions happen in the **mitochondria**, which is why very active cells, such as muscle cells and sperm cells, contain many mitochondria.
bullets: Word equation: **glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water** (energy released).
Balanced symbol equation: **C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O**.
Location: begins in the cytoplasm but most of the reactions happen in the **mitochondria**.
It is the main way cells release energy because it is far more efficient than anaerobic respiration.
Oxygen reaches cells by **diffusion** from the blood; glucose comes from digested food carried in the plasma.
The carbon dioxide made diffuses out of cells into the blood and is breathed out at the lungs.

callouts.p: Respiration that **uses oxygen** to break down glucose completely into carbon dioxide and water, releasing a **large amount of energy**.

core.p: **Anaerobic respiration** happens **without oxygen**. In animal cells, such as muscle cells during hard exercise, glucose is broken down only **partially** into **lactic acid**. It happens in the **cytoplasm**, not the mitochondria.
bullets: Word equation (animals): **glucose → lactic acid** (energy released).
No oxygen is used and **no carbon dioxide** is produced.
It releases **much less energy** per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration because the glucose is **not fully broken down**: a lot of chemical energy is still stored in the lactic acid.
It happens when muscles are working so hard that the heart and lungs cannot supply oxygen fast enough for aerobic respiration alone.
It is useful because it releases energy **quickly** for a short burst of activity, such as a sprint.
**Lactic acid** builds up in muscles and contributes to **muscle fatigue**: muscles contract less strongly and may ache.

callouts.p: Respiration **without oxygen**, in which glucose is only partially broken down, releasing **much less energy** than aerobic respiration.

core.p: Lactic acid cannot stay in the muscles. After exercise it is carried in the blood to the **liver**, where it is broken down. This requires **oxygen**, so you keep breathing hard and your heart rate stays high after you stop exercising.
bullets: **Oxygen debt** is the extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down the lactic acid that built up during anaerobic respiration.
This is why breathing rate and depth stay high for a while after a sprint.
Fitter people recover faster because their heart and lungs deliver oxygen more efficiently, so they build up less lactic acid in the first place.
In the liver lactic acid can be converted back to glucose or oxidised to carbon dioxide and water.

callouts.p: The amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to **break down the lactic acid** produced by anaerobic respiration.

core.h: Anaerobic respiration in plants and fungi (yeast)
core.p: Plant cells and **yeast** (a single-celled fungus) can also respire anaerobically, but the products are different from animals. Glucose is broken down into **ethanol** and **carbon dioxide**. In yeast this is called **fermentation**.
bullets: Word equation (plants and yeast): **glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide** (energy released).
Like anaerobic respiration in animals, it happens in the cytoplasm and releases much less energy than aerobic respiration.
Plant roots in waterlogged soil respire anaerobically because the soil has little oxygen; the ethanol is toxic, so roots can die.
Yeast fermentation is used in **bread making** (carbon dioxide makes dough rise) and in **brewing beer and wine** (ethanol is the alcohol).
Yeast respires aerobically when oxygen is present and anaerobically when it is not.

callouts.t: Animals do not make carbon dioxide anaerobically
callouts.p: Only anaerobic respiration in **plants and fungi** produces carbon dioxide. Anaerobic respiration in **animals** produces **only lactic acid**.

core.p: This comparison is exactly what spec point 8.10 asks for. Learn the table and be ready to give both a similarity and differences.
bullets: **Similarities**: both release energy from glucose; both are exothermic; both are controlled by enzymes; both happen in living cells; both use glucose as the substrate.
**Difference in oxygen**: aerobic needs oxygen, anaerobic does not.
**Difference in products**: aerobic makes carbon dioxide and water; anaerobic makes lactic acid (animals) or ethanol and carbon dioxide (plants and yeast).
**Difference in energy**: aerobic releases much more energy per glucose molecule because glucose is fully broken down.
**Difference in location**: aerobic mostly in mitochondria; anaerobic in the cytoplasm.
**Difference in duration**: aerobic can continue for a long time; anaerobic can only be used for short periods in animals because lactic acid builds up.

callouts.p: In a 'compare' question every point needs **both** types: for example 'aerobic releases **more** energy **than** anaerobic', not just 'aerobic releases a lot of energy'.

core.p: The key grade 9 idea is **complete versus incomplete breakdown** of glucose. In aerobic respiration glucose is broken down all the way to carbon dioxide and water, which store very little chemical energy, so almost all the available energy is released. In anaerobic respiration the products (lactic acid or ethanol) are still energy-rich molecules, so much of the energy stays locked inside them.
bullets: Evidence: ethanol burns as a fuel, which shows it still contains lots of stored chemical energy.
Lactic acid can be converted back to glucose in the liver, again showing the energy was not all released.
Oxygen is needed for the final reactions in the mitochondria that release most of the energy, so without oxygen those stages cannot happen.
Because anaerobic respiration releases less energy per glucose, cells using it must break down glucose much faster to release energy at the same rate.

callouts.p: Anaerobic respiration releases less energy **because glucose is only partially broken down**, so energy remains stored in the lactic acid or ethanol.

core.h: Switching between aerobic and anaerobic respiration
core.p: Cells use aerobic respiration whenever there is enough oxygen. When the oxygen supply cannot keep up with demand, they also respire anaerobically. This explains changes seen during exercise.
bullets: During exercise, muscles need more energy, so the **rate of respiration increases**.
Breathing rate and depth increase to take in more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide.
Heart rate increases to deliver oxygen and glucose to muscles faster and remove carbon dioxide faster.
If demand is still greater than supply, muscle cells top up energy release with **anaerobic respiration**, making lactic acid.
After exercise, the oxygen debt is repaid by continued deep breathing.

callouts.p: Exercise questions reward a chain: more contraction → more energy needed → more respiration → more oxygen and glucose needed → higher heart and breathing rate.

core.p: Students often confuse respiration with breathing and with photosynthesis. Being clear about the differences avoids lost marks.
bullets: **Breathing** is a physical process moving air; **respiration** is a chemical reaction in cells.
**Photosynthesis** is **endothermic** (takes in energy from light); **respiration** is **exothermic** (releases energy).
Aerobic respiration is roughly the reverse of photosynthesis: photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen.
Plants do both: they photosynthesise only in the light but respire all the time.

analogy.t: Glucose as a bar of chocolate shared out
analogy.p: Think of a glucose molecule as a big bar of chocolate (stored energy). Aerobic respiration is like eating the whole bar, square by square: you get all the energy, and the wrapper and crumbs left over (carbon dioxide and water) are worthless. Anaerobic respiration is like taking a quick bite when you are in a rush and throwing the rest of the bar away: it is fast, but most of the chocolate (energy) is still in the leftovers (lactic acid or ethanol). Oxygen is the time you need to sit down and eat properly. Where it breaks down: in a cell the 'leftover' lactic acid is not wasted forever, because the liver later uses oxygen to break it down, and the energy in respiration is released in many small enzyme-controlled steps rather than in bites.

terms.d: An exothermic reaction occurring continuously in living cells that releases energy from glucose for metabolic processes.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the products store less energy than the reactants.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, such as photosynthesis.
The sum of all the chemical reactions that happen in a cell or organism.
Respiration using oxygen, breaking glucose down completely into carbon dioxide and water and releasing a large amount of energy.
Respiration without oxygen, breaking glucose down partially and releasing much less energy than aerobic respiration.
Organelles in which most of the reactions of aerobic respiration take place.
The jelly-like part of the cell where anaerobic respiration takes place.
The product of anaerobic respiration in animal cells such as muscle cells.
An alcohol produced with carbon dioxide during anaerobic respiration in plants and yeast.
Anaerobic respiration in yeast, producing ethanol and carbon dioxide.
The extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down the lactic acid produced by anaerobic respiration.
Muscles becoming tired and contracting less efficiently, partly due to lactic acid build-up.
Movement of substances against a concentration gradient using energy released by respiration.
The sugar used as the main substrate (fuel) for respiration.
A biological catalyst; each step of respiration is controlled by a specific enzyme.

mistakes.w: Respiration produces energy.
mistakes.r: Respiration releases (transfers) energy; energy cannot be created.

mistakes.w: Respiration is breathing.
mistakes.r: Respiration is a chemical reaction in cells; breathing is the movement of air in and out of the lungs.

mistakes.w: Anaerobic respiration in muscles produces lactic acid and carbon dioxide.
mistakes.r: Anaerobic respiration in animals produces only lactic acid; carbon dioxide is only produced anaerobically in plants and yeast.

mistakes.w: Plants only respire at night.
mistakes.r: Plants respire all the time, day and night; they photosynthesise only in the light.

mistakes.w: Anaerobic respiration produces no energy.
mistakes.r: Anaerobic respiration releases energy, but much less per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration.

mistakes.w: Respiration is endothermic because it needs energy.
mistakes.r: Respiration is exothermic: it transfers energy to the surroundings.

mistakes.w: Aerobic respiration releases more energy because it uses more glucose.
mistakes.r: It releases more energy per glucose molecule because glucose is completely broken down to carbon dioxide and water.

mistakes.w: Anaerobic respiration happens in the mitochondria.
mistakes.r: Anaerobic respiration happens in the cytoplasm; aerobic respiration happens mainly in the mitochondria.

mistakes.w: Oxygen debt is oxygen you owe because you stopped breathing.
mistakes.r: Oxygen debt is the extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down lactic acid.

exam.q: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
model: Glucose + oxygen on the left
Carbon dioxide + water on the right
exam.tip: Do not write 'energy' as a product in place of a substance; it can be added in brackets.

exam.q: Name the product of anaerobic respiration in human muscle cells.
model: Lactic acid
exam.tip: Only one product: no carbon dioxide.

exam.q: Name the organelle where most aerobic respiration takes place.
model: Mitochondria / mitochondrion
exam.tip: Not nucleus or chloroplast.

exam.q: Explain why respiration is described as an exothermic reaction.
model: Energy is transferred / released to the surroundings
Products have less stored energy than reactants / heat is given out
exam.tip: Use 'transferred to the surroundings'.

exam.q: Give two uses of the energy released by respiration in animals.
model: Muscle contraction
Any one of: active transport / synthesis of large molecules (e.g. proteins) / maintaining body temperature
exam.tip: Be specific; 'for growing' alone may not score.

exam.q: Write the word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast.
model: Glucose on the left
Ethanol + carbon dioxide on the right
exam.tip: Both products needed for the second mark.

exam.q: Explain why anaerobic respiration releases less energy than aerobic respiration.
model: Glucose is not completely broken down / only partially broken down
Energy remains stored in lactic acid / ethanol
exam.tip: The grade 9 word is 'partially'.

exam.q: Explain why a sprinter continues to breathe heavily after a race.
model: Anaerobic respiration occurred during the race producing lactic acid
Oxygen is needed to break down the lactic acid (in the liver)
This is the oxygen debt being repaid
exam.tip: Mention lactic acid, oxygen and oxygen debt.

exam.q: Compare aerobic respiration with anaerobic respiration in animal cells.
model: Aerobic uses oxygen; anaerobic does not
Aerobic produces carbon dioxide and water; anaerobic produces lactic acid
Aerobic releases more energy (per glucose) than anaerobic
Aerobic occurs in mitochondria; anaerobic in cytoplasm
Both use glucose / both release energy / both are exothermic
exam.tip: Each mark needs a comparison of both processes.

exam.q: Germinating peas were placed in a vacuum flask with a thermometer. A second flask contained boiled peas. Explain the expected results.
model: Temperature rises in flask with germinating peas
Because living peas respire which is exothermic / releases heat
Boiled peas are dead / enzymes denatured so no respiration, so temperature does not rise
exam.tip: Explain the control as well as the test.

exam.q: Explain how the body responds to exercise in terms of respiration, and discuss the advantages and disadvantages of anaerobic respiration to an athlete.
model: Muscles contract more so need more energy
Rate of respiration increases
Heart rate and breathing rate increase to supply more oxygen and glucose and remove carbon dioxide
If oxygen supply is insufficient, muscles respire anaerobically
Advantage: releases energy quickly without oxygen for short bursts
Disadvantage: releases much less energy per glucose
Lactic acid builds up causing muscle fatigue / pain
Oxygen debt must be repaid after exercise
exam.tip: Structure: response, then advantages, then disadvantages.

worked.q: A muscle cell respiring aerobically releases about 19 times more energy per glucose molecule than when respiring anaerobically. If anaerobic respiration releases 120 kJ from a sample of glucose, how much energy would aerobic respiration release from the same amount of glucose? Explain what this means for the cell.
steps: Energy from aerobic = 19 × energy from anaerobic.
So the cell would need to break down about 19 times more glucose anaerobically to release the same energy.
This is because anaerobic respiration only partially breaks down glucose, leaving energy stored in lactic acid.
worked.ans: 2280 kJ; anaerobic respiration is much less efficient, so glucose would be used up far faster and lactic acid would build up.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why plant roots die if the soil becomes waterlogged for a long time.
steps: Water fills the air spaces between soil particles, so there is little oxygen in the soil.
Root cells cannot carry out enough aerobic respiration, so they respire anaerobically.
Anaerobic respiration in plants produces ethanol and carbon dioxide; ethanol is toxic to cells.
Less energy is released, so there is too little energy for active transport of mineral ions, and cells are damaged by ethanol.
worked.ans: Lack of oxygen forces anaerobic respiration, which releases little energy and makes toxic ethanol, so root cells cannot absorb minerals and eventually die.

bio_edx.7.7.summary: In this core practical you measure the **rate of respiration** of small living organisms, such as woodlice, maggots or germinating seeds, using a **respirometer**. **Soda lime** absorbs the carbon dioxide they give out, so as they take in oxygen for aerobic respiration the gas volume and pressure in the tube fall and a drop of **coloured liquid moves along a capillary tube** towards them. The distance the drop moves in a set time shows the volume of oxygen used, so you can find how a factor such as **temperature** affects the rate, using a control tube of glass beads and treating the animals ethically.

core.p: The aim is to **investigate the rate of respiration in living organisms**, usually by finding how **temperature** affects the rate of oxygen uptake. Respiration is controlled by **enzymes**, so changing temperature should change the rate. Because we cannot see respiration happening, we measure something that changes because of it: the **oxygen used up**.
bullets: Typical organisms: **woodlice**, **maggots** (fly larvae), **germinating peas or seeds**, or yeast.
Independent variable: usually **temperature** (for example 10, 20, 30, 40 °C using water baths).
Dependent variable: **distance moved by the coloured liquid** in a set time (or the volume of oxygen taken in).
Control variables: species and **mass/number of organisms**, volume of soda lime, size of tube, diameter of capillary tube, time allowed, time to acclimatise.
The organisms must be alive and respiring aerobically for the method to work.

callouts.p: The respirometer measures the **rate of oxygen uptake**. Carbon dioxide is removed by soda lime, so any change in gas volume is caused only by **oxygen being used** in aerobic respiration.

core.p: A simple respirometer is a sealed boiling tube connected to a **capillary tube** with a scale. Organisms sit on a **wire gauze** platform above some **soda lime**. A small drop of **coloured liquid** is placed in the capillary tube so you can see the gas volume change.
bullets: **Boiling tube** sealed with a bung so no air can enter or leave except through the capillary tube.
**Soda lime** in the bottom of the tube to **absorb carbon dioxide** released by the organisms.
**Wire gauze** to keep the organisms off the soda lime, which is corrosive and would harm them.
**Capillary tube** containing a **drop of coloured liquid**, with a **ruler or scale** alongside to measure how far it moves.
A **syringe** or three-way tap can be used to push the drop back to the start, so the apparatus can be reset between readings.
A **water bath** keeps the tube at a constant, chosen temperature; a thermometer checks it.

callouts.p: Exams may ask you to label the soda lime, gauze, organisms and capillary tube, or to say what each part does. Learn the function of each, not just its name.

core.p: This is the most commonly tested explanation. Follow the chain of reasoning step by step.
bullets: The organisms carry out **aerobic respiration**, taking in **oxygen** from the air in the tube.
They release **carbon dioxide**, but it is immediately **absorbed by the soda lime**.
So overall the **volume of gas** in the sealed tube **decreases**.
This lowers the **pressure** inside the tube below atmospheric pressure.
The higher atmospheric pressure outside pushes the coloured liquid **along the capillary tube towards the organisms**.
The **distance moved** in a set time is proportional to the **volume of oxygen used**, so a faster movement means a **higher rate of respiration**.

callouts.p: In aerobic respiration the volume of carbon dioxide released is about the same as the oxygen taken in. Without soda lime the gas volume would hardly change and the liquid would **barely move**.

core.p: A clear, ordered method is often worth 6 marks. Include equipment, what you control, what you measure and how you repeat.
bullets: Wear **eye protection** and **gloves**. Place a measured amount of **soda lime** in a boiling tube and add a wire gauze platform above it.
Weigh a set **mass** of woodlice (or count a set number) and place them on the gauze.
Insert the bung with the capillary tube attached. Introduce a small drop of coloured liquid into the capillary tube.
Place the tube in a **water bath** at the first temperature (for example 15 °C) and leave it for about **5 minutes** so the air inside reaches the bath temperature and the organisms **acclimatise**.
Mark the starting position of the drop and start the **stopwatch**. After a set time (for example **5 minutes**) record the **distance moved** in mm.
Use the syringe to reset the drop, then **repeat** at least **three times** at this temperature and calculate a **mean**, ignoring anomalies.
Repeat the whole procedure at different temperatures (for example 20, 25, 30 °C), using the same organisms or a fresh, equal mass.
Set up a **control** tube with **glass beads** of the same volume as the organisms, at each temperature.
Return the organisms **unharmed** to their habitat afterwards.

callouts.p: Examiners reward specific quantities: 'leave for 5 minutes', 'measure distance moved in 5 minutes', 'repeat 3 times', '5 g of woodlice'.

core.p: A **control tube** contains everything except the living organisms. They are replaced with **glass beads** of the **same volume**, or with **dead (boiled) seeds** if seeds are being used.
bullets: It shows that the movement of the liquid is caused **only by the organisms respiring**, not by something else.
Changes in **temperature** or **atmospheric pressure** in the room could make the gas expand or contract and move the drop.
Any movement seen in the control can be **subtracted** from the movement in the test tube to give a more accurate result.
The glass beads take up the same volume so the volume of air in both tubes is the same.
A better design links the control tube to the test tube with a U-tube (a differential respirometer), so changes in room conditions cancel out.

callouts.p: An identical tube with **glass beads of the same volume** instead of living organisms, to show that any movement of the coloured liquid is due to **respiration of the organisms**.

core.p: The simplest rate is the **distance moved by the drop per unit time**. For a more accurate measure you can convert distance into **volume of oxygen** using the formula for the volume of a cylinder, because the inside of the capillary tube is a long thin cylinder.
bullets: **Rate = distance moved ÷ time taken**, in mm per minute (mm/min).
**Volume of oxygen = π × r² × distance moved**, where r is the internal **radius** of the capillary tube (in mm, so volume is in mm³).
Rate of oxygen uptake = volume ÷ time, in mm³ per minute.
To compare organisms of different sizes, divide by mass: rate per gram, for example mm³ per g per min.
Remember radius = diameter ÷ 2; using the diameter by mistake gives an answer four times too big.
Subtract any movement in the control tube before calculating the rate.

callouts.p: Rate = distance ÷ time. Volume = π r² × distance.

core.p: For woodlice, maggots or germinating seeds, the rate of respiration **increases as temperature increases**, up to an **optimum**, and then **decreases** at high temperatures.
bullets: Respiration is controlled by **enzymes**.
As temperature rises, molecules have **more kinetic energy**, so enzymes and substrates collide more often and more **enzyme-substrate complexes** form, so the rate increases.
Above the optimum, the **active site** of the enzymes changes shape and the enzymes **denature**, so the rate decreases.
Woodlice and maggots are **ectotherms**: their body temperature changes with the surroundings, so the water bath temperature directly controls their enzyme activity.
At very high temperatures the organisms would be harmed, which is why experiments do not usually go above about 35 to 40 °C.

callouts.p: Explanations must mention **enzymes**, **kinetic energy / collisions** and, above the optimum, **denaturing** of the **active site**.

core.p: Every core practical answer should consider **hazards**, the **risk** they pose and how to **reduce** it.
bullets: **Soda lime is corrosive** and an irritant: wear **eye protection** and **gloves**, and do not touch it with bare hands.
Hot water in water baths can scald: use thermostatically controlled baths and do not go above the planned temperature.
Glass boiling tubes and capillary tubes can break and cut: handle carefully and clear up breakages with a dustpan, not hands.
Wash hands after handling organisms such as maggots or woodlice.

callouts.t: Hazard is not the same as risk
callouts.p: A **hazard** is something that could cause harm (corrosive soda lime). The **risk** is the chance of harm happening. Always give the **precaution** too.

core.p: Because this practical uses **living animals**, you must treat them with respect and minimise any harm or stress. Edexcel mark schemes regularly reward these points.
bullets: Use the **minimum number** of organisms needed to get valid results.
Keep the **wire gauze** in place so organisms never touch the corrosive soda lime.
Do **not** use **extreme temperatures** that would harm or kill them.
Do not leave them in the sealed tube for **too long**, because oxygen would run out.
Handle them **gently** (for example with a soft paintbrush) and **return them to their natural habitat** after the investigation.
Using germinating seeds avoids some ethical issues because plants do not feel pain.

callouts.t: Two ethical points for two marks
callouts.p: Safe answers: **gauze stops contact with soda lime**, **return organisms to habitat**, **avoid extreme temperatures**, **do not leave sealed for long**.

core.p: Grade 9 answers can evaluate the method and suggest improvements. Think about anything that could change the gas volume apart from respiration, and anything that makes readings hard to take.
bullets: **Acclimatisation time**: allow the tube to reach the bath temperature before timing, or warming gas will expand and push the drop the wrong way.
**Airtight seal**: check the bung for leaks, for example with petroleum jelly; a leak means the drop will not move properly.
**Same mass of organisms** each time, because more organisms use more oxygen.
**Repeats and means** reduce the effect of random errors and help spot anomalies.
**Narrower capillary tube**: the drop moves further for the same volume of oxygen, making small changes easier to measure (higher resolution).
**Activity of organisms**: woodlice move around more at some temperatures, which affects respiration rate; keeping them in the dark can reduce this.
Use a **differential respirometer** with a control linked by a U-tube so room temperature and pressure changes cancel out.

core.p: The same respirometer can investigate other variables. The logic is always the same: change one factor, keep everything else the same, measure the drop movement.
bullets: **Type of organism**: compare woodlice with maggots, using equal mass, and calculate rate per gram.
**Germinating versus dry seeds**: germinating seeds respire much faster because they are growing and need lots of energy.
**Mass of organisms**: more mass gives a faster drop movement, so rate must be compared per gram.
**Yeast**: the effect of sugar concentration or temperature can be measured by counting bubbles of carbon dioxide or using a gas syringe instead.

analogy.t: A sealed room with a carbon dioxide scrubber
analogy.p: Imagine people in a sealed room with a machine (the soda lime) that sucks all the carbon dioxide out of the air. As people breathe in oxygen, the air in the room slowly gets less and less, so the room's pressure drops. If there were a small door with a ping-pong ball in its keyhole (the coloured drop), the outside air would push the ball inwards. The more people there are and the harder they work (more respiration), the faster the ball moves. Where it breaks down: real people would also be harmed as oxygen falls, which is why in the practical you only seal the organisms in for a short time, and a respirometer measures tiny volumes in a thin tube rather than a whole room.

terms.d: Apparatus used to measure the rate of respiration of living organisms by measuring oxygen uptake.
How quickly respiration happens, measured here as the volume of oxygen used per unit time.
A corrosive chemical that absorbs carbon dioxide from the air in the respirometer.
A very narrow glass tube in which a drop of coloured liquid moves as gas volume changes.
A mesh platform that keeps organisms away from the soda lime.
An identical tube with glass beads of the same volume instead of organisms, to show movement is due to respiration.
The variable you change, usually temperature in this practical.
The variable you measure, the distance moved by the coloured liquid in a set time.
A variable kept the same so it does not affect the results, such as mass of organisms.
Leaving the apparatus in the water bath so the organisms and air reach the set temperature before measuring.
An animal whose body temperature changes with the surroundings, such as a woodlouse.
When an enzyme's active site changes shape at high temperature so it can no longer bind its substrate.
The temperature at which the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction is highest.
The total of repeat readings divided by the number of readings, ignoring anomalies.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the others, usually due to an error.
Something that could cause harm, such as corrosive soda lime.

mistakes.w: The soda lime absorbs oxygen.
mistakes.r: Soda lime absorbs carbon dioxide; the organisms use up the oxygen.

mistakes.w: The liquid moves because the organisms produce carbon dioxide.
mistakes.r: The liquid moves because oxygen is used up and carbon dioxide is absorbed, so gas volume and pressure in the tube decrease.

mistakes.w: The liquid moves away from the organisms.
mistakes.r: The liquid moves towards the organisms because pressure inside the tube falls.

mistakes.w: The control is the tube at room temperature.
mistakes.r: The control is an identical tube with glass beads of the same volume instead of living organisms.

mistakes.w: The gauze is to let air through.
mistakes.r: The gauze stops the organisms touching the corrosive soda lime.

mistakes.w: At high temperatures the enzymes are killed.
mistakes.r: Enzymes are not alive; they denature as the active site changes shape.

mistakes.w: Volume = π × d² × distance using the diameter.
mistakes.r: Volume = π × r² × distance, where r is the radius (half the diameter).

mistakes.w: Repeating makes the results more accurate.
mistakes.r: Repeating and calculating a mean makes results more reliable/repeatable and helps identify anomalies.

mistakes.w: Use as many woodlice as possible to get a big reading.
mistakes.r: Use the minimum number needed, with the same mass each time, for ethical reasons and fair comparison.

exam.q: State the purpose of the soda lime in the respirometer.
model: To absorb carbon dioxide (released by the organisms)
exam.tip: Not oxygen.

exam.q: State why the woodlice are placed on a wire gauze.
model: To stop them coming into contact with the (corrosive) soda lime
exam.tip: Link to safety of the organisms.

exam.q: Give the independent and dependent variables in an investigation into the effect of temperature on respiration rate of woodlice.
model: Independent: temperature
Dependent: distance moved by coloured liquid (in a set time) / volume of oxygen used
exam.tip: Be specific about what is measured.

exam.q: Explain why the coloured liquid moves towards the woodlice.
model: Woodlice use oxygen in (aerobic) respiration
Carbon dioxide released is absorbed by soda lime
So volume of gas / pressure in tube decreases, drawing the liquid towards them
exam.tip: Mention both gases and the pressure change.

exam.q: Describe a suitable control for this experiment and explain why it is needed.
model: Tube with glass beads of same volume instead of woodlice
To show that movement is due to respiration / to account for changes in temperature or pressure
exam.tip: 'Same volume' is needed for the first mark.

exam.q: The drop moved 18 mm in 6 minutes. Calculate the rate of movement.
model: = 3 mm/min
exam.tip: Include units.

exam.q: Give two ethical considerations when using woodlice in this investigation.
model: Use gauze to prevent contact with soda lime
Any one: return to habitat / avoid extreme temperatures / do not leave sealed for long / handle carefully / use minimum number
exam.tip: Ethics is about the animals, not about your own safety.

exam.q: Give one hazard in this practical and a precaution.
model: Soda lime is corrosive
Wear gloves / eye protection
exam.tip: Hazard and precaution must match.

exam.q: Explain why the rate of respiration of the woodlice increased between 10 °C and 30 °C.
model: Respiration is controlled by enzymes
Higher temperature gives molecules more kinetic energy
More collisions / more enzyme-substrate complexes formed per second
exam.tip: Woodlice are ectotherms, so their body temperature follows the water bath.

exam.q: The capillary tube has an internal diameter of 1 mm. The drop moved 20 mm in 5 minutes. Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake in mm³ per minute.
model: Radius = 0.5 mm
Volume = π × 0.5² × 20 = 15.7 mm³
Rate = 15.7 ÷ 5 = 3.1 mm³/min
exam.tip: Halve the diameter first.

exam.q: Describe a method to investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of respiration of maggots.
model: Set up a respirometer with soda lime, gauze and a set mass of maggots, sealed with a bung and capillary tube
Place in a water bath at a set temperature and leave to acclimatise (e.g. 5 minutes)
Measure distance moved by coloured liquid in a set time (e.g. 5 minutes)
Reset with syringe and repeat (3 times) to calculate a mean
Repeat at a range of temperatures (e.g. 10 to 35 °C)
Use a control tube with glass beads of same volume
Control variables: same mass of maggots, same volume of soda lime, same capillary tube
Safety and ethics: gloves and goggles for soda lime, return maggots unharmed
exam.tip: Six-mark method questions need equipment, measurements, control variables, repeats and a control.

worked.q: A student measured the distance moved by the coloured liquid for woodlice at 25 °C in three repeats of 5 minutes: 23 mm, 25 mm and 41 mm. The control drop moved 1 mm in 5 minutes. Calculate the mean corrected rate of respiration in mm/min.
steps: Identify the anomaly: 41 mm does not fit the pattern, so ignore it.
Correct using the control: 24 − 1 = 23 mm.
Rate = 23 mm ÷ 5 min = 4.6 mm/min.
worked.ans: 4.6 mm/min

worked.q: Germinating peas of mass 4 g were placed in a respirometer. The drop moved 30 mm in 10 minutes. The capillary tube has a radius of 0.4 mm. Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake per gram of peas in mm³ per g per minute. Use π = 3.14.
steps: Volume of oxygen = π × r² × distance = 3.14 × 0.4² × 30.
Rate = 15.07 ÷ 10 = 1.507 mm³ per minute.
Per gram = 1.507 ÷ 4 = 0.377 mm³ per g per minute.
worked.ans: 0.38 mm³ per g per min (2 significant figures)

worked.q: Model answer: Suggest why the drop moved slightly away from the tube in the first minute after the respirometer was placed in a 35 °C water bath.
steps: The apparatus had not acclimatised; the air inside was cooler than the bath.
As the air warmed it expanded, increasing the gas volume.
This pushed the drop away from the organisms, hiding the effect of oxygen uptake.
Improvement: leave the tube in the bath for about 5 minutes before starting the timing.
worked.ans: The gas inside was expanding as it warmed up, so the student should allow an acclimatisation period before taking readings.

bio_edx.7.8.summary: Cardiac output is the volume of blood pumped out of one ventricle of the heart every minute, and it is calculated with the equation **cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate**. Stroke volume is the volume of blood pushed out of the ventricle in one beat, and heart rate is the number of beats per minute. You must be able to use and rearrange this equation, handle units (cm³, dm³, beats per minute), and explain why cardiac output rises during exercise and why trained athletes have a larger stroke volume and a lower resting heart rate.

core.p: Every cell needs a steady supply of **oxygen** and **glucose** for **aerobic respiration**, and needs **carbon dioxide** removed. The heart is the pump that keeps blood moving through the double circulatory system, so the amount of blood it pumps per minute controls how fast these substances are delivered and removed.
bullets: Blood carries oxygen bound to haemoglobin in red blood cells
Plasma carries glucose to cells and carries carbon dioxide away
A higher cardiac output means **more blood reaches the muscles per minute**, so more oxygen and glucose arrive per minute
More respiration releases more energy for muscle contraction
Faster blood flow also removes carbon dioxide and heat more quickly

callouts.p: Cardiac output links the heart to respiration: more blood per minute means more oxygen and glucose delivered per minute.

core.p: There are three linked quantities. You need to know each definition and its unit, because exam questions often give you two and ask you to work out the third.
bullets: **Heart rate** = the number of times the heart beats per minute (beats per minute, bpm)
**Stroke volume** = the volume of blood pumped out of the left ventricle in one heartbeat (cm³ or cm³ per beat)
**Cardiac output** = the volume of blood pumped out of the left ventricle per minute (cm³ per minute or dm³ per minute)
Typical resting values for an adult: heart rate about 70 bpm, stroke volume about 70 cm³, cardiac output about 5 dm³ per minute

head: Quantity
Meaning
Usual unit
rows: cm³ per minute or dm³ per minute

callouts.p: The volume of blood pumped by the heart (one ventricle) per minute.
The volume of blood pumped out of the heart (left ventricle) in one beat.

core.p: The equation makes sense if you think about units: if each beat pushes out a certain volume, and there are a certain number of beats each minute, multiplying them gives the volume per minute.
bullets: **cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate**
cm³ per beat x beats per minute = cm³ per minute
The 'beats' cancel, leaving volume per minute
Learn this equation by heart: do not rely on it being given in the exam

callouts.p: CO = SV x HR. Always write the equation first in a calculation answer, because it often earns credit.

fig.cap: Formula triangle for cardiac output. Cover the quantity you want: cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate; stroke volume = cardiac output / heart rate; heart rate = cardiac output / stroke volume.

core.p: You must be able to rearrange the equation to find any one of the three quantities. Dividing both sides by one quantity leaves the other on its own.
bullets: **stroke volume = cardiac output / heart rate**
**heart rate = cardiac output / stroke volume**
Check your answer is sensible: resting stroke volume is usually 50 to 100 cm³ and resting heart rate 50 to 100 bpm
If you get a stroke volume of 5 cm³ or 5000 cm³, you have probably mixed up units

callouts.p: After rearranging, put your answer back into CO = SV x HR to check you get the value you started with.

core.p: Unit errors are the most common way to lose marks. Cardiac output is often given in dm³ per minute, but stroke volume is given in cm³, so you may need to convert first.
bullets: **1 dm³ = 1000 cm³** (1 dm³ is the same as 1 litre)
To convert dm³ to cm³, multiply by 1000; to convert cm³ to dm³, divide by 1000
Example: 5.6 dm³ per minute = 5600 cm³ per minute
Heart rate must be in beats per **minute**; if you are given beats in 15 seconds, multiply by 4
Always give a unit with your final answer unless the question already shows it on the answer line

callouts.p: Dividing a cardiac output in dm³ by heart rate gives stroke volume in dm³, e.g. 0.07 dm³. Convert to cm³ (70 cm³) if the answer line asks for cm³.

core.p: Each heartbeat sends a surge of blood through the arteries, which you can feel as a **pulse**. Counting the pulse therefore gives the heart rate.
bullets: Feel the pulse at the **wrist** (radial artery) or the **neck** (carotid artery), where an artery runs close to the skin over a bone
Use two fingers, not the thumb (the thumb has its own pulse)
Count beats for 60 seconds, or for 15 seconds and multiply by 4
Repeat and calculate a mean to improve reliability
Heart rate can also be measured with a heart rate monitor or from an ECG trace

callouts.p: Counting for 15 s is quicker but any counting error is multiplied by 4, so counting for a full minute is more accurate.

core.h: Heart rate from the time of one beat
core.p: Sometimes you are given a trace (such as an ECG) showing the time for one heartbeat instead of a count. Since there are 60 seconds in a minute, dividing 60 by the time for one beat gives beats per minute.
bullets: **heart rate (bpm) = 60 / time for one beat (s)**
Example: one beat every 0.8 s gives 60 / 0.8 = 75 bpm
If a trace shows several beats, measure the time for several beats and divide by the number of beats to get a more accurate time per beat
A shorter time per beat means a higher heart rate

core.p: During exercise the muscles respire faster, so they need more oxygen and glucose and produce more carbon dioxide. The body responds by increasing **both heart rate and stroke volume**, which multiplies up to a much bigger cardiac output.
bullets: Muscles contract more, so the **rate of respiration** increases
More oxygen and glucose must be delivered per minute; more carbon dioxide must be removed
Heart rate increases, and the heart contracts more strongly so stroke volume increases
Cardiac output can rise from about 5 dm³/min at rest to over 20 dm³/min in hard exercise
Breathing rate and depth also increase to take in more oxygen at the lungs
If oxygen supply still cannot keep up, muscles also respire **anaerobically**, producing lactic acid and an **oxygen debt**
After exercise, heart rate stays raised for a while to carry lactic acid to the liver and repay the oxygen debt

callouts.p: More exercise, more respiration, more oxygen and glucose needed, higher heart rate and stroke volume, higher cardiac output, more blood delivered to muscles per minute.

core.p: Regular endurance training makes the **heart muscle larger and stronger**, especially the wall of the left ventricle. A stronger ventricle pushes out more blood with each contraction, so the stroke volume is bigger.
bullets: Athletes have a **larger stroke volume** at rest (for example 100 cm³ instead of 70 cm³)
Because each beat moves more blood, they need **fewer beats** to supply the same cardiac output, so their **resting heart rate is lower**
At rest, the body's oxygen demand is similar, so resting cardiac output is about the same for athletes and non-athletes
During maximum exercise, an athlete's larger stroke volume gives a **much higher maximum cardiac output**, delivering more oxygen to muscles
Athletes' heart rates also return to resting more quickly after exercise (faster recovery)

callouts.p: Do not say an athlete's heart beats slower 'so it pumps less blood'. Resting cardiac output is about the same because the larger stroke volume makes up for the lower heart rate.

core.p: It helps to picture one minute of heart activity as repeated identical pumps, each delivering one stroke volume of blood.
bullets: Each contraction of the left ventricle pushes one stroke volume into the **aorta**
The number of contractions in a minute is the heart rate
Total volume in that minute is the cardiac output
The right ventricle pumps the same volume per minute to the lungs, because blood flows in a continuous loop

core.p: Heart rate is not fixed. It changes to match the body's demand for oxygen. Knowing the causes helps you explain data in exam questions.
bullets: **Exercise** increases heart rate to supply more oxygen to respiring muscles
**Adrenaline** (released by the adrenal glands in fight or flight) increases heart rate and blood flow to muscles
Fitness: fitter people have lower resting heart rates
Age, stress, body temperature and illness can also affect heart rate
In an investigation, control variables such as age, sex, fitness and the type and length of exercise

core.p: Calculation questions are usually 2 or 3 marks. Marks come for the correct equation or substitution, the correct answer, and sometimes the correct unit or rounding.
bullets: Write the equation, then substitute the numbers with units
Convert units **before** substituting
Show your working so you can gain method marks even if the final answer is wrong
Give the answer to the number of significant figures or decimal places asked for
When asked to calculate a percentage change: (new - original) / original x 100

callouts.p: Cardiac output rising from 5.0 to 20.0 dm³/min is (20.0 - 5.0) / 5.0 x 100 = 300% increase, not 400%.

analogy.p: Imagine a person filling a tank by throwing buckets of water. The size of each bucket is the **stroke volume**, the number of buckets thrown per minute is the **heart rate**, and the total water delivered per minute is the **cardiac output**. To deliver more water you can throw faster or use bigger buckets, which is exactly what the heart does in exercise. A trained athlete is like someone with a bigger bucket: they can throw fewer times per minute and still deliver the same amount. The analogy breaks down because the heart does not refill from an outside tap: the blood goes round a closed loop and comes back to the heart, and the ventricle does not empty completely with each beat.

terms.d: The number of heartbeats per minute, measured in beats per minute (bpm).
The volume of blood pumped out of the left ventricle in one heartbeat, usually in cm³.
The volume of blood pumped out of the left ventricle per minute; cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate.
The surge of blood felt in an artery each time the ventricles contract; counting it gives the heart rate.
The chamber of the heart with the thickest muscular wall, which pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta to the body.
The main artery that carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body.
The heart rate when the body is at rest, about 60 to 80 bpm in an average adult.
The time taken for heart rate to return to its resting value after exercise; shorter in fitter people.
Respiration using oxygen: glucose + oxygen to carbon dioxide + water, releasing energy.
Respiration without oxygen; in muscles glucose is converted to lactic acid, releasing less energy.
The extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down the lactic acid produced by anaerobic respiration.
Cubic decimetre, a unit of volume equal to 1000 cm³ or 1 litre.
A hormone from the adrenal glands that increases heart rate in a fight or flight response.
A system in which blood passes through the heart twice per circuit: once to the lungs and once to the body.

mistakes.w: Cardiac output is the number of times the heart beats per minute.
mistakes.r: That is heart rate. Cardiac output is the **volume of blood** pumped per minute.

mistakes.w: Stroke volume is how much blood is in the heart.
mistakes.r: Stroke volume is the volume of blood **pumped out of the left ventricle in one beat**.

mistakes.w: Cardiac output = heart rate / stroke volume.
mistakes.r: Cardiac output = stroke volume **x** heart rate.

mistakes.w: 5.6 / 80 = 0.07 so stroke volume is 0.07 cm³.
mistakes.r: Convert 5.6 dm³ to 5600 cm³ first: 5600 / 80 = 70 cm³.

mistakes.w: Counted 18 beats in 15 seconds so heart rate is 18 bpm.
mistakes.r: Multiply by 4 to get beats per minute: 72 bpm.

mistakes.w: An athlete has a low resting heart rate because their heart is weaker or they need less oxygen.
mistakes.r: The athlete's heart muscle is **larger and stronger**, so **stroke volume is bigger** and fewer beats are needed for the same cardiac output.

mistakes.w: Heart rate increases in exercise to make more energy.
mistakes.r: Heart rate increases to **deliver more oxygen and glucose to muscles** for **respiration**, which releases energy (energy is not made).

mistakes.w: During exercise only heart rate increases.
mistakes.r: Both heart rate **and stroke volume** increase, so cardiac output increases.

mistakes.w: Answer given without units, or as cm³ when it should be cm³ per minute.
mistakes.r: Cardiac output is a volume **per minute**, e.g. cm³/min or dm³/min.

exam.q: State what is meant by the term cardiac output.
model: The volume of blood pumped by the heart / left ventricle per minute
exam.tip: Include both 'volume of blood' and 'per minute'.

exam.q: State the equation that links cardiac output, stroke volume and heart rate.
model: Cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate
exam.tip: Write it in words or as CO = SV x HR.

exam.q: A student has a stroke volume of 75 cm³ and a heart rate of 68 beats per minute. Calculate the student's cardiac output.
model: = 5100 cm³ per minute
exam.tip: Show the substitution to get the method mark.

exam.q: A man's cardiac output is 6.3 dm³ per minute and his heart rate is 90 beats per minute. Calculate his stroke volume in cm³.
model: 6.3 dm³ = 6300 cm³
stroke volume = 6300 / 90
exam.tip: Convert dm³ to cm³ before dividing.

exam.q: A woman counted 21 pulse beats in 15 seconds. Her stroke volume is 80 cm³. Calculate her cardiac output in dm³ per minute.
model: heart rate = 21 x 4 = 84 bpm
cardiac output = 80 x 84 = 6720 cm³/min
= 6.72 dm³/min
exam.tip: Two conversions here: time and volume.

exam.q: An ECG shows one heartbeat every 0.75 seconds. Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute.
model: = 80 beats per minute
exam.tip: Heart rate = 60 / time for one beat.

exam.q: Explain why heart rate increases during exercise.
model: Muscles contract more so need more energy
so rate of (aerobic) respiration increases
more oxygen and glucose needed by muscles (per minute)
more carbon dioxide must be removed
higher heart rate increases cardiac output / blood flow to muscles
exam.tip: Link heart rate to blood flow, then to oxygen, then to respiration.

exam.q: A trained athlete has a resting heart rate of 50 bpm and a resting cardiac output of 5000 cm³/min. An untrained person has a resting heart rate of 72 bpm and the same cardiac output. Explain the difference in heart rate.
model: Athlete's stroke volume is larger (100 cm³ compared with about 69 cm³)
because athlete's heart muscle / left ventricle wall is larger / stronger
so fewer beats are needed to pump the same volume of blood per minute
exam.tip: Use the numbers: calculate both stroke volumes to support your answer.

exam.q: During exercise a runner's stroke volume rises from 80 cm³ to 120 cm³ and heart rate rises from 60 to 160 bpm. Calculate the percentage increase in cardiac output.
model: resting CO = 80 x 60 = 4800 cm³/min
exercise CO = 120 x 160 = 19200 cm³/min
exam.tip: Percentage change = change / original x 100.

exam.q: Describe how a student could investigate the effect of exercise on heart rate and use the results to compare cardiac output. (6 marks)
model: Measure resting pulse at wrist or neck with two fingers
count beats for 60 s (or 15 s x 4) and repeat for a mean
carry out a set exercise, e.g. step-ups for 3 minutes at a fixed rate
measure pulse immediately after and every minute until it returns to resting
control variables such as same person / age / type and duration of exercise
cardiac output can be calculated as stroke volume x heart rate if stroke volume is known
higher heart rate after exercise shows higher cardiac output, delivering more oxygen to muscles
exam.tip: Six-mark method answers need a clear sequence plus control variables and how the data are used.

worked.q: A patient has a cardiac output of 4.8 dm³ per minute and a stroke volume of 60 cm³. Calculate the heart rate.
steps: Write the rearranged equation: heart rate = cardiac output / stroke volume
Convert units: 4.8 dm³ = 4.8 x 1000 = 4800 cm³
Substitute: heart rate = 4800 / 60
Calculate: 80
Check: 60 x 80 = 4800 cm³/min, which is 4.8 dm³/min
worked.ans: 80 beats per minute

worked.q: Before training, a cyclist has a resting heart rate of 75 bpm and a stroke volume of 68 cm³. After a year of training, resting cardiac output is unchanged but stroke volume is 85 cm³. Calculate the new resting heart rate and explain the change.
steps: Resting cardiac output before = 68 x 75 = 5100 cm³/min
After training cardiac output is still 5100 cm³/min
New heart rate = 5100 / 85 = 60 bpm
Explanation: training makes the heart muscle, especially the left ventricle wall, larger and stronger
Each beat pumps more blood, so fewer beats per minute supply the same volume
worked.ans: 60 beats per minute; the heart rate falls because the larger stroke volume delivers the same cardiac output with fewer beats.

worked.q: A student counts 26 beats in 20 seconds. Her stroke volume is 70 cm³. Calculate her cardiac output in dm³ per minute to 2 significant figures.
steps: Heart rate = 26 x 3 = 78 beats per minute (20 s x 3 = 60 s)
Cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate = 70 x 78
= 5460 cm³ per minute
Convert: 5460 / 1000 = 5.46 dm³ per minute
Round to 2 significant figures: 5.5
worked.ans: 5.5 dm³ per minute
